title: Re-check cart price, quantity, discounts and role claims on the server every time
hypothesis: If every cart price, quantity, discount code and role claim is re-checked on the server for each request, then price manipulation and privilege fraud drop because a rewritten client request can no longer be trusted.

signal.check: A developer can change a price, quantity, discount amount or role field in the browser network tab and the order or admin action still goes through.

risk.note: None; this only adds checks the server should already run.

prerequisites: Access to the checkout, cart and admin API code
steps: List every place price, quantity, discount, credit or role is read from a request.
For each, add a server-side lookup or recompute step instead of trusting the submitted value.
Test by editing the request in dev tools or a proxy and confirming the server rejects or ignores it.
Log any request where the server value disagrees with the submitted value.

test.method: Replay a modified cart, discount or role request against staging with a proxy tool
test.measure: share of tampered requests the server rejects or silently recomputes
test.read_point: after the fix ships, before it goes live

title: Triage a security finding by whether a working exploit exists, not by its label
hypothesis: If findings are sorted by whether a working exploit hits a live customer-facing surface, then urgent fixes ship first because effort is not wasted on latent issues with no path to harm yet.

signal.check: A scan, report or researcher note lists findings with no urgency ranking, or everything is treated as equally urgent.

risk.note: None; this is a triage rule, not a code change.

prerequisites: A way findings arrive: a scan tool, a report form or a researcher channel
steps: For each new finding, check whether a working exploit exists against a live surface today.
If yes, treat as urgent: fix, add a compensating control, or take the feature offline.
If no working exploit exists, schedule as normal work plus a compensating control (extra logging, a rate limit).
Record the decision and date for each finding.

test.method: Review the last 10 findings triaged this way against how they were actually handled
test.measure: share of urgent-exploit findings fixed within the disclosure SLA

title: Never rely on one security control alone; assume each one can fail
hypothesis: If every sensitive action is protected by at least two independent controls, then a single failure (a leaked password, a compromised dependency) does not turn into a full account or store compromise.

signal.check: A sensitive action (admin login, payout change, API access) has exactly one control protecting it, for example MFA alone with no permission check or logging behind it.

risk.note: Adding a second layer rarely breaks the first.

prerequisites: A list of the store's sensitive actions and their current controls
steps: List every sensitive action: admin login, payout change, API key issue, price override.
For each, name the controls protecting it today.
Add a second, independent layer to any action with only one (for example, permission check plus logging behind MFA).
Note in the runbook that MFA, a WAF rule or any single control is assumed breachable, not a stop.

test.method: Walk through each sensitive action and confirm two independent controls exist
test.measure: count of sensitive actions with only one control, before and after
test.read_point: at the next quarterly security review

title: Pick the weaker control the team will actually keep on over the strong one they will disable
hypothesis: If a control decision favors what the team can run continuously over what looks strictest on paper, then coverage stays up over time instead of lapsing because a stricter setting got switched off after one lockout.

signal.check: A strict setting (a lockout policy, a hard block rule) was turned off after causing a lockout or false positive and nothing replaced it.

risk.note: This is a decision rule, not a technical change.

prerequisites: A list of controls that were tried and then turned off
steps: List any control turned off in the last year because it locked out real users or staff.
For each, choose a version the team can run continuously (detection instead of hard block, monitor before enforce).
Document why the stricter version was rejected so it is not retried the same way.

test.method: Review the control log after 90 days
test.measure: whether the replacement control is still on and unmodified

title: Let staff and developers work freely in a sandbox and enforce security only at the promotion step
hypothesis: If security friction is removed from day-to-day development and staging work and enforced only when code or a setting is promoted to the live store, then people stop routing around controls because the controls no longer block normal work.

signal.check: Developers or staff share workarounds for a security step (shared logins, disabled 2FA, copied API keys) because it blocks routine work.

risk.note: None; this only moves where the gate sits.

prerequisites: A staging or sandbox environment separate from production
steps: Confirm staff and developers have an isolated environment for normal work with light friction.
Move the strict checks (approval, MFA, review) to the point code or a setting reaches the live store.
Reject any promotion that skips the gate.

test.method: Ask staff which security step they route around and why, then check whether it moved to the promotion gate
test.measure: number of reported workarounds
test.read_point: one quarter after the gate moves

title: Run a quarterly four-pillar security audit with a named owner per pillar
hypothesis: If privacy, integrity, authentication and non-repudiation each get a named owner and a quarterly review, then gaps get caught on a schedule instead of only after an incident.

signal.check: No one owns a security pillar by name, or the last review of privacy, integrity, authentication or non-repudiation controls was more than a quarter ago.

risk.note: This is a review process, not a live change.

prerequisites: A list of current controls to sort into the four pillars
steps: Sort every current control into privacy, integrity, authentication or non-repudiation.
Assign one owner per pillar.
Put a review of each pillar on the quarterly calendar.
Note that passing this review is not the same as PCI DSS compliance.

test.method: Check whether each pillar had a completed review last quarter
test.measure: count of pillars reviewed on schedule

title: Match login defenses to the 3 credential-guessing patterns, not one generic rule
hypothesis: If login defenses separately cover brute force, credential stuffing and password spraying, then account takeover drops because each pattern is caught by the specific control it needs (per-account limits, breach-list checks, per-source velocity limits).

signal.check: Login defenses are one generic rate limit with no separate check for many passwords on one account, breached password reuse, or one password tried across many accounts.

risk.note: None if thresholds are sized from real traffic first.

prerequisites: Login failure logs per username and per IP
steps: Separate login failure logs into 3 patterns: many passwords on 1 account, known-breach passwords on many accounts, 1 password across many accounts.
Add a breach-list check at signup and password change to block credential stuffing.
Add a per-source velocity limit to catch password spraying.
Keep the per-account rate limit for brute force.

test.method: Review login failure logs for 2 weeks after the split defenses ship
test.measure: count of accounts taken over, by attack pattern

title: Extend bot and rate-limit monitoring to API endpoints, not only customer-facing pages
hypothesis: If checkout, inventory and account APIs get the same bot monitoring as storefront pages, then API-targeted attacks are caught sooner because most advanced bot traffic already targets APIs, not pages.

signal.check: Bot monitoring or a WAF is configured for storefront pages but the API inventory has no equivalent monitoring or rate limits.

expected_effect.size: 44% of advanced bot traffic targets API endpoints (source-cited)

risk.note: None; this adds coverage rather than removing anything.

prerequisites: An API inventory (rule for R111)
steps: List every API endpoint: checkout, inventory, account, search.
Confirm each has the same rate limiting and bot monitoring as an equivalent page.
Flag any endpoint with no monitoring at all.

test.method: Compare bot and WAF logs for pages versus APIs over one month
test.measure: share of API endpoints with active monitoring
test.read_point: one month after adding API coverage

title: Track the reserved-to-converted inventory ratio during drops to catch hoarding bots
hypothesis: If the store tracks how many reserved carts during a drop never convert, then inventory-hoarding bots are caught fast because a high claim-to-no-conversion ratio is a clear signal, not guesswork.

signal.check: A drop or limited-stock launch shows carts reserved far above the units that convert to paid orders, with no report tracking this ratio.

risk.note: Reporting only; no live change to checkout.

prerequisites: Cart reservation and order data for launch windows
steps: Pull cart reservation counts and paid conversion counts for the next drop.
Compute the ratio of reserved-and-abandoned to reserved-and-converted.
Flag any SKU or window where the ratio is far above the store's normal rate.
Investigate flagged windows for bot patterns before the next drop.

test.method: Compare the ratio across 2 drops, one with monitoring and one without
test.measure: reserved-to-converted ratio

does_not_apply_when: No limited drops, flash launches or frequently sold-out SKUs

title: Confirm and name the store's DDoS mitigation layer before a peak traffic event
hypothesis: If the store names its CDN or DDoS provider and confirms coverage before a sale or launch, then a flood attack is less likely to lock out real customers during the highest-value traffic window.

signal.check: No one can name the store's current DDoS mitigation layer, or it has never been tested before a peak event.

risk.note: Confirmation only unless a new provider is added.

prerequisites: Knowledge of hosting model: hosted platform or self-hosted
steps: On a hosted platform, confirm what protection the platform provides by default.
On self-hosted, name the CDN or DDoS provider and confirm the plan covers the store's traffic tier.
Add a check of this before each major sale or launch to the peak-season checklist.

test.method: Ask the hosting or CDN provider to confirm current DDoS coverage in writing
test.measure: written confirmation on file

title: Prefer a hosted, non-editable checkout and treat every checkout script as a skimming risk
hypothesis: If the store keeps checkout on the platform's hosted, non-editable page and audits any script that can reach it, then digital skimming (Magecart) risk drops because HTTPS does not stop a script that runs on the payment page itself.

signal.check: Any script, pixel, chat widget or app injects code onto the checkout or payment page, or the checkout page has been custom-coded.

risk.note: Removing a script can break a feature; test after each removal.

prerequisites: A crawl of the checkout page listing every script
steps: Crawl the checkout page and list every script, pixel, tag and iframe.
Confirm the store uses the platform's hosted checkout rather than a customized one.
Flag any script on checkout that is not required to take payment.
Remove or move flagged scripts off the checkout page.

test.method: Recrawl checkout after changes and diff the script list
test.measure: count of non-payment scripts on checkout
test.read_point: after each app or pixel install

title: Vet a third-party script's access and privileges before adding it anywhere on the site
hypothesis: If every new script is checked for what it can read and do before it goes live, then a compromised or malicious script vendor cannot silently gain full page privileges because the check happens before install, not after an incident.

signal.check: A widget, chat tool, retention popup or ad pixel was added without checking what data it can read or what requests it can make.

risk.note: Adds a review step; does not remove anything by itself.

prerequisites: A gate in the app or script install process
steps: Before installing any script, list what it can read (DOM, cookies) and what requests it can make.
Confirm the vendor's own security practices are documented, not assumed.
Log the decision and reviewer with the app inventory.
Re-check any script whose vendor changes ownership.

test.method: Review the last 5 script installs against this checklist
test.measure: share of installs with a documented privilege review

title: Watch for lookalike and IDN homograph domains impersonating the brand
hypothesis: If the store watches for lookalike or IDN homograph domains copying its name, then customer and staff phishing losses drop because the fake domain gets reported and taken down before it collects logins or card data.

signal.check: No one currently searches for domains that look like the brand's own domain, and a customer or staff phishing report has never been checked against a lookalike domain.

risk.note: None; this is monitoring and reporting, not a live change.

prerequisites: The brand's own domain and common misspellings listed
steps: List the brand's domain and likely lookalike or IDN homograph variants.
Search periodically for registered domains matching those variants.
Report and request takedown of any confirmed lookalike used for phishing.
Train staff and customers on tab-nabbing and lookalike sender tells.

test.method: Run the lookalike domain search monthly and track findings
test.measure: count of lookalike domains found and taken down

title: Watch marketplaces and social ads for counterfeit listings using the brand's name and photos
hypothesis: If the store periodically searches marketplaces and social ads for its own name, logo and product photos, then counterfeit and card-harvesting storefronts get reported and removed before they damage trust or take payment data under the brand's name.

signal.check: No one currently searches marketplaces or social platforms for listings using the brand's name, logo or product photos without authorization.

risk.note: None; monitoring and takedown requests only.

prerequisites: Brand name, logo and key product photos on file for search
steps: Search major marketplaces and social ad libraries for the brand's name, logo and product photos monthly.
Confirm whether a match is an authorized reseller or a counterfeit.
File a takedown request for confirmed counterfeits.
Log each case for pattern tracking.

test.method: Track takedown requests filed and resolved over a quarter
test.measure: count of counterfeit listings removed

title: Lock the domain registrar account and audit DNS for dangling records
hypothesis: If the registrar account has MFA, a short editor list and no dangling CNAMEs, then DNS hijacking and subdomain takeover become far harder because the weakest hop (the registrar login) is closed.

signal.check: The registrar account has no MFA, an editor list longer than needed, or a DNS export shows a CNAME pointing at a service that no longer exists.

risk.note: None once MFA and editor changes are confirmed working.

prerequisites: Access to the registrar account
steps: Enable MFA on the registrar account.
Review and shorten the list of people who can edit DNS.
Export the DNS zone and check every CNAME for a target that still exists.
Remove or fix any dangling CNAME.

test.method: Re-export the DNS zone after cleanup and confirm no dangling records remain
test.measure: count of dangling CNAMEs found and fixed

title: Audit non-login endpoints for timing or content differences that leak hidden state
hypothesis: If endpoints beyond login (order status, loyalty balance, gift card checks) are checked for timing or response differences tied to hidden state, then account enumeration and data leaks drop because these overlooked side channels get closed too.

signal.check: An endpoint's response time, content or status code differs depending on whether an account, order or balance exists, and no one has checked for this.

risk.note: None; testing and equalizing response behavior.

prerequisites: A list of endpoints beyond login that check account or order existence
steps: List endpoints that look up an account, order, gift card or loyalty balance.
Test each for a timing or content difference between an existing and non-existing target.
Equalize the response and timing where a difference is found.

test.method: Time and compare responses for existing vs non-existing targets on each endpoint
test.measure: count of endpoints with a closed timing or content gap

title: Build the fraud business case from a cited cost range, then replace it with the brand's own numbers
hypothesis: If a fraud-control business case uses a cited cost-per-dollar range plus the brand's own chargeback fees, refunds and staff hours, then spending decisions are grounded in real cost instead of one vendor's marketing number.

signal.check: A fraud-control spend decision cites a single vendor statistic with no brand data and no mention of the false-decline cost on the other side.

expected_effect.size: cited range $4.61 to $5.13 per $1 of fraud, both vendor-cited and period-specific

risk.note: This is a reporting exercise, not a live change.

prerequisites: Chargeback fees, refund totals and staff review hours for the last period
steps: Pull chargeback fees, refunds on fraud orders, lost goods, and staff review hours for the last quarter.
Show the cited $4.61 to $5.13 per dollar range alongside the brand's own computed number.
Include the false-decline cost (lost sales from over-blocking) in the same case.
Use the brand number, not the vendor range, for the final decision.

test.method: Compare the brand's computed fraud cost to the cited range next quarter
test.measure: brand fraud cost per dollar of confirmed fraud

title: Track return rate by SKU and customer to catch wardrobing and serial-returner fraud
hypothesis: If return rate is tracked by SKU and by customer, then wardrobing and serial-returner losses drop because repeat high-value or worn-and-returned patterns get flagged for review before a refund goes out.

signal.check: Return and refund decisions are made per order with no SKU-level or customer-level pattern check.

risk.note: A wrongly flagged genuine customer creates a support cost; review before denying.

prerequisites: Order and return data with SKU and customer id
steps: Pull return rate by SKU for the last 90 days.
Pull return count and value by customer for the same window.
Flag SKUs and customers above the store's normal range.
Review flagged cases before approving future refunds.

test.method: Compare fraud-flagged return value before and after tracking starts
test.measure: value of flagged high-risk returns caught before refund

does_not_apply_when: No return policy, or a category with no meaningful return volume

title: Track COD refusal rate by pincode and phone number and require confirmation above a value threshold
hypothesis: If COD refusal rate is tracked by pincode and phone number and a confirmation call or OTP is required above a value threshold, then losses from fake-name COD orders and repeat no-shows drop because high-risk orders get a second check before shipping.

signal.check: COD orders ship with no confirmation step and refusal or no-show rate by pincode or phone number is not tracked.

risk.note: Extra confirmation step can add friction; set the value threshold carefully.

prerequisites: Order data with pincode, phone number and COD flag
steps: Pull COD refusal and no-show rate by pincode and phone number for the last quarter.
Set a value threshold above which a confirmation call or OTP is required before dispatch.
Flag repeat-refusal phone numbers or pincodes for extra review.
Track refusal rate after the confirmation step starts.

test.method: Compare COD refusal rate before and after the confirmation step
test.measure: COD refusal rate

does_not_apply_when: No cash-on-delivery option offered

title: Write down which security duties the hosted platform covers and which the merchant still owns
hypothesis: If the store writes down which controls Shopify (or another hosted platform) covers versus which ones the merchant owns, then gaps like weak admin passwords, phishing and app permissions stop being assumed away as 'the platform's job'.

signal.check: No written list exists of what the platform covers versus what the merchant owns, and a security question gets answered with 'the platform handles that' without checking.

risk.note: Documentation only.

prerequisites: Current Shopify plan and feature terms
steps: List platform-covered items: infrastructure, servers, payment systems, checkout code.
List merchant-owned items: credentials, staff access, app permissions, customer data handling.
Confirm each merchant-owned item has a current control.
Revisit the list whenever the plan or platform changes.

test.method: Review the list against the next security baseline audit
test.measure: count of merchant-owned items with no control

title: List every security duty a self-hosted store owns alone, with no platform safety net
hypothesis: If a self-hosted store writes down that it alone owns TLS, PCI validation, patching, firewalls, backups and DDoS protection, then these duties stop getting skipped on the assumption 'the platform handles it', which only applies to hosted stores.

signal.check: A self-hosted store cannot name who owns TLS renewal, patching, firewall rules, backups or DDoS protection.

risk.note: Documentation only.

prerequisites: A list of the store's current hosting and infrastructure stack
steps: List every duty: TLS issuance/renewal, PCI validation, OS and app patching, firewall/WAF rules, backups, DDoS protection.
Name an owner (in-house or contracted) for each.
Budget for independent PCI validation, roughly $1,000 to $10,000 a year per the cited estimate.
Flag any duty with no owner as an open risk.

test.method: Review the ownership list at the next security baseline audit
test.measure: count of duties with a confirmed owner

title: Ban card numbers from notes, email, chat and shared documents
hypothesis: If staff are trained and systems are checked to keep card numbers out of order notes, email, chat and shared documents, then the most common human-error exposure closes because platform PCI coverage never extended to these channels anyway.

signal.check: A sample of support tickets, order notes or shared documents turns up a full or partial card number.

risk.note: None; this is a policy and training change.

prerequisites: Access to sample support tickets, order notes and shared documents
steps: Sample recent support tickets, order notes and shared documents for card numbers.
Purge any found and note the exposure event.
Train support staff to redirect any customer who sends card details to checkout instead.
Add a policy line: card data is never asked for or accepted outside checkout.

test.method: Re-sample tickets and documents 90 days after training
test.measure: count of card numbers found outside checkout

title: Get the PCI DSS SAQ type and scope confirmed by the acquirer in writing
hypothesis: If the store gets its PCI DSS SAQ type and validation route confirmed in writing by the acquirer instead of assuming it from transaction volume, then every payment control that follows rests on the right scope instead of a guess.

signal.check: The store assumes it is PCI Level 4 with only an annual SAQ because it does under 20,000 transactions a year, with no written confirmation from the acquirer.

risk.note: None; this is a confirmation step.

prerequisites: Contact with the acquirer or payment brand
steps: Ask the acquirer or payment brand in writing for the SAQ type and validation route.
Map where card data is captured, processed and stored across store, apps and support.
File the written determination where it can be found for the next audit.
Re-confirm on any acquirer or processor change.

test.method: Confirm the written determination is on file
test.measure: written PCI determination on file, yes or no

title: Verify a payment gateway's PCI, tokenization and 3DS 2.0 support directly with the provider
hypothesis: If a gateway's PCI DSS certification, tokenization and 3DS 2.0 support are confirmed directly with the provider instead of from its marketing page, then a chosen or kept gateway actually meets today's payment security bar.

signal.check: A gateway's PCI, tokenization or 3DS 2.0 claims come only from its marketing page and have never been reverified directly with the provider.

risk.note: Confirmation only.

prerequisites: Current or candidate gateway contact
steps: Ask the gateway provider directly for its current PCI DSS certification level.
Confirm tokenization and 3DS 2.0 support in writing.
Re-verify on a set cadence (yearly) since certifications and versions change.

test.method: File the provider's written confirmation and set a re-verify reminder
test.measure: written confirmation on file
test.read_point: yearly and on any gateway change

title: Confirm what a platform's SOC 1 or SOC 2 audit actually covers before citing it
hypothesis: If the store confirms a platform's SOC audit covers only the platform's own environment before repeating the claim to a client, then the store avoids overstating its own compliance based on someone else's audit.

signal.check: A client report or pitch cites the platform's SOC 1/SOC 2 audit as if it covers the merchant's own store setup.

risk.note: None; this only affects wording in reports.

prerequisites: The platform's current SOC audit documentation
steps: Read the platform's SOC 1/SOC 2 report scope statement.
Confirm it covers only the platform's environment, not merchant configuration or apps.
Correct any client-facing material that overstates what the audit covers.

test.method: Review the next client report for this claim before it ships
test.measure: count of reports with an accurate SOC scope statement

title: Verify Shopify's default security claims against current documentation before repeating them
hypothesis: If claims like 'PCI compliant by default', 'free TLS on every plan' and 'Plus has the same default security' are checked against current Shopify documentation before being written into a client report, then the store avoids repeating a vendor statement that may have changed.

signal.check: A client report repeats a Shopify default security claim with no date or verification link, and no one has checked current Shopify docs.

risk.note: None; a documentation check.

prerequisites: Current Shopify help center or documentation access
steps: Before writing any Shopify default-security claim into a report, check current Shopify documentation.
Note the check date next to the claim.
Flag any claim that could not be confirmed as `[web check]` rather than stating it as fact.

test.method: Spot-check the last client report for unverified Shopify claims
test.measure: share of Shopify security claims with a documented verification date

title: Serve the entire site over HTTPS, not only the login and checkout pages
hypothesis: If every page, not only login and checkout, is served over HTTPS, then session cookie theft and the 'Not secure' warning both go away, because a session cookie is as valuable as the password it protects.

signal.check: Any page on the site loads over plain HTTP, or a browser shows a 'Not secure' warning anywhere on the site.

risk.note: Mixed-content errors can appear; fix asset URLs as they surface.

prerequisites: A valid TLS certificate for every hostname the store uses
steps: Request every page and hostname over HTTP and confirm it redirects to HTTPS.
Fix any page that loads a resource over plain HTTP (mixed content).
Recheck home, product, cart, checkout and account pages with dev tools open.

test.method: Load key pages in a fresh browser profile and check for HTTPS and no mixed-content warnings
test.measure: share of pages with no HTTP or mixed-content warning
test.read_point: right after the fix, then quarterly

title: Set Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, Path and a bounded expiry on every session cookie
hypothesis: If every session cookie carries Secure, HttpOnly, an explicit SameSite value, Path=/ and a bounded expiry, then a stolen or reused cookie is far harder to exploit because it cannot be read by script, sent over plain HTTP, or replayed forever.

signal.check: A custom login's Set-Cookie header is missing Secure, HttpOnly or SameSite, or has no expiry.

risk.note: None; standard cookie hardening.

prerequisites: A custom login with a server-side session store
steps: Set Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, Path=/ and a bounded Max-Age (about 30 days, renewed per visit) on the session cookie.
Confirm the cookie is inspected via Set-Cookie headers, not guessed.
When clearing the cookie, repeat every attribute with a past expiry, since a partial clear leaves the original cookie intact.

test.method: Inspect Set-Cookie headers on login and confirm all attributes are present
test.measure: share of session cookies with all required attributes

does_not_apply_when: Shopify or another platform that sets its own session cookie

title: Replace any identity or role data in a cookie with an opaque, revocable session id
hypothesis: If the session cookie holds only an opaque random id looked up in a server-side table, instead of identity or role data (signed or not), then logout and password change actually kill a stolen cookie, because a signed value can be copied but never revoked.

signal.check: A custom login stores a user id, role or other identity data directly in a cookie, signed or not.

risk.note: Requires a migration window; keep the old session store readable for one cookie lifetime.

prerequisites: A server-side session store
steps: Store session_id -> user data server-side; the cookie holds only the opaque id.
Delete the server-side row on logout; offer 'log out other devices' by deleting other rows.
Invalidate all sessions for a user on password change or a compromise signal.
Keep the old session store readable for one cookie lifetime while migrating.

test.method: Copy a session cookie, log out, and replay the copied cookie
test.measure: replay succeeds or fails after logout

title: Generate session ids from about 128 bits of cryptographic randomness
hypothesis: If session ids come from a cryptographic random source with about 128 bits of entropy, never sequential and never bound to IP or user agent, then session guessing and fixation attacks become computationally infeasible.

signal.check: A custom login's session ids are sequential, short, or derived from predictable values like IP or timestamp.

risk.note: None; a generation function change.

prerequisites: A custom login with server-generated session ids
steps: Switch session id generation to a cryptographic RNG with about 128 bits of output.
Confirm ids are never sequential or derived from IP or user agent.
Rotate any existing predictable session ids on next login.

test.method: Sample generated session ids and check for randomness and length
test.measure: entropy of a sample of generated ids

title: Reserve signed cookies for values a user may see but never needs revoked individually
hypothesis: If signed (non-opaque) cookies are used only for values like a discount flag that the server never needs to revoke per-user, then the store avoids the mistake of treating a signed cookie as a secure session, since a signed value can still be copied to another browser.

signal.check: A signed cookie is used to carry something the server may need to revoke for one user, such as a login or entitlement state.

risk.note: None; a usage-scope rule.

prerequisites: An inventory of what each cookie carries
steps: List what each cookie carries and whether the server ever needs to revoke it per user.
Keep signed cookies only for values like promo flags or preferences.
Move any identity or entitlement data to an opaque, server-revocable session id.

test.method: Review the cookie inventory for any signed cookie carrying revocable state
test.measure: count of signed cookies carrying identity or entitlement data

title: Isolate each app or login flow on its own subdomain instead of relying on cookie Path
hypothesis: If the login flow and each separate app on the domain get their own subdomain, then a compromised sibling app cannot read the login cookie, because cookie Path is not a real security boundary and a subdomain can otherwise read its parent's cookies.

signal.check: More than one app or login flow shares the same domain and relies on cookie Path to separate them.

risk.note: Moving a login flow to a subdomain can require a migration and redirect plan.

prerequisites: DNS control for the domain
steps: List every app and login flow sharing the domain.
Put the login flow and any sensitive app on its own subdomain.
Confirm cookies are scoped to the subdomain, not the parent domain, where isolation is the goal.

test.method: Attempt to read the login cookie from a sibling app after the split
test.measure: whether the sibling app can read the login cookie

does_not_apply_when: A store with only one app on its domain

title: Choose SameSite=Lax as the default session cookie setting
hypothesis: If the session cookie defaults to SameSite=Lax and only a truly isolated flow uses Strict, then CSRF exposure drops without breaking OAuth or payment-provider return flows that need a top-level navigation to carry the cookie.

signal.check: The session cookie has no SameSite attribute set, or Strict is used broadly and breaks a login-with-provider or payment-return flow.

risk.note: Test every cross-site return flow after the change.

prerequisites: A custom login and session cookie
steps: Set SameSite=Lax on the session cookie by default.
Reserve Strict only for a cookie with no legitimate cross-site top-level navigation.
Test OAuth login and payment-provider return flows after the change.

test.method: Test every cross-site return flow (OAuth, payment provider) after setting SameSite
test.measure: pass or fail on each return flow

title: Add a stateless CSRF token to every state-changing request, even with SameSite set
hypothesis: If every state-changing request (cart update, checkout, address, password, API key) carries a stateless CSRF token, then one forgotten SameSite exception or old-browser session cannot reopen a CSRF hole.

signal.check: State-changing endpoints rely on SameSite alone with no CSRF token as a second layer.

risk.note: Token verification can run in log-only mode for one release before enforcing.

prerequisites: A list of every state-changing endpoint
steps: List every state-changing endpoint: cart, checkout, address, email, password, API key.
Compute the token as HMAC(session id, server secret); embed as a hidden field.
Verify the token on every state-changing request and reject on mismatch.
Run verification in log-only mode for one release before enforcing.

test.method: Submit a hidden auto-submitting form from a second real hostname
test.measure: whether the forged request is rejected

title: Convert every state-changing action from GET to POST plus a token
hypothesis: If logout, cart clear, discount apply and settings toggles are converted from GET to POST plus a token, then a marketing email link or an image tag on another site can no longer fire a state change on a shopper's behalf.

signal.check: A grep of routes shows logout, cart clear, discount apply or a settings toggle responding to a plain GET request.

risk.note: Check that no marketing email or bookmark relies on the old GET link.

prerequisites: A route list for the store's custom endpoints
steps: Grep routes for any state change responding to GET.
Convert each to POST with a CSRF token.
Check marketing email templates for any link that used to trigger a GET-based action.

test.method: Load a marketing-style link (an img tag pointing at the old GET endpoint) and confirm nothing changes
test.measure: count of GET endpoints still changing state

title: Route every HTTP method to its own handler and reject unexpected methods including HEAD
hypothesis: If GET and POST are registered as fully separate routes and every other method including HEAD is explicitly rejected, then a framework's implicit CSRF hook cannot be silently bypassed by a method it does not cover.

signal.check: A route uses a two-way if GET else POST pattern, or the framework's CSRF hook has never been confirmed to cover every method including HEAD.

risk.note: None; a routing hardening change.

prerequisites: Access to the route definitions
steps: Register GET and POST as separate routes, not a single branch.
Add an explicit reject for any other method including HEAD.
Send a HEAD request to every state-changing endpoint and confirm it is rejected or harmless.

test.method: Send a HEAD request to each state-changing endpoint
test.measure: share of endpoints that reject or safely ignore HEAD

title: Test SameSite and CSRF fixes across two real hostnames, not two ports on localhost
hypothesis: If SameSite and CSRF fixes are tested from a genuinely different hostname instead of a second localhost port, then a passing test actually proves the fix works, because the cookie site check ignores port but not hostname.

signal.check: The last CSRF or SameSite test used two ports on localhost instead of two real hostnames.

risk.note: None; a test setup change.

prerequisites: A staging environment with a second real hostname available
steps: Set up a second real hostname (not a second port) for CSRF testing.
Re-run every prior SameSite or CSRF test from that hostname.
Fix any test that only passed because it ran on localhost.

test.method: Re-run the CSRF test suite from a genuinely separate hostname
test.measure: pass or fail count on the retest

title: Deny framing on checkout, cart, account and admin pages
hypothesis: If checkout, cart, account and admin pages send an anti-framing header (X-Frame-Options or CSP frame-ancestors), then clickjacking against these state-changing pages is blocked, because JavaScript frame-busting alone is not reliable.

signal.check: Loading checkout, cart, account or admin in an iframe from a different origin renders the page instead of blank.

risk.note: Remove the header only for a path that deliberately needs to be framed.

prerequisites: Ability to set response headers, or confirm what the platform already sets
steps: Set X-Frame-Options DENY (or SAMEORIGIN) and CSP frame-ancestors with the same value on state-changing pages.
On Shopify, check what the platform already sets before adding a merchant-side header.
Load each protected page in an iframe from a test origin and confirm it renders blank.

test.method: Frame each protected page from a test origin
test.measure: whether the framed page renders blank

title: Allow-list the Origin header on checkout and payment-method endpoints
hypothesis: If checkout, address book and payment-method-update endpoints check the browser-set Origin header against an allow-list, then cross-site form submissions from a foreign page are rejected outright, without relying on the spoofable Referer or User-Agent headers.

signal.check: Checkout, address book or payment-method endpoints accept a request with no Origin check, or rely on Referer or User-Agent instead.

risk.note: None; adds a header check.

prerequisites: A list of endpoints that must reject foreign submissions
steps: List checkout, address book and payment-method endpoints.
Allow-list the store's own Origin values on each.
Reject any request with a missing or foreign Origin on these endpoints.
Confirm normal checkout still works after the change.

test.method: Submit a cross-origin request to each listed endpoint and confirm rejection
test.measure: share of listed endpoints rejecting foreign Origin

title: Set Referrer-Policy on any page holding a password reset, order status or unsubscribe link
hypothesis: If pages holding a capability URL (password reset, order status with token, unsubscribe link) set Referrer-Policy, then that token does not leak to the next site the shopper clicks through to.

signal.check: A password reset, order status or unsubscribe page with a token in the URL has no Referrer-Policy set and links out to another site.

risk.note: None; a header addition.

prerequisites: A list of pages with a token in the URL
steps: List every page whose URL carries a password reset, order status or unsubscribe token.
Set Referrer-Policy to strip or limit the referrer on these pages.
Confirm outbound links from these pages no longer pass the token in the referrer.

test.method: Click an outbound link from a token-bearing page and inspect the referrer sent
test.measure: whether the token appears in the outbound referrer

title: Put personalized assets and loyalty balances at unguessable per-user URLs
hypothesis: If avatars, order status images, loyalty badges and balance pages live at unguessable per-user URLs instead of predictable ids, then hotlinking and ambient-cookie leaks stop exposing one shopper's personal or loyalty data to a foreign page.

signal.check: A personalized asset (avatar, order status image, loyalty badge or balance) is reachable at a predictable id, such as an incrementing customer number.

risk.note: None; URLs are regenerated, not removed.

prerequisites: A list of personalized sub-resources and their current URL scheme
steps: List every personalized asset: avatar, order status image, loyalty badge, balance page.
Replace predictable ids with unguessable per-user tokens in the URL.
Hold loyalty account passwords to the same policy as checkout accounts.
Confirm hotlinking an old predictable URL no longer returns personal data.

test.method: Try to guess or increment a URL to reach another user's personalized asset
test.measure: whether a guessed id returns another user's data

title: Escape every user-rendered field by context using the framework's auto-escaping layer
hypothesis: If every user-rendered field (reviews, Q&A, wishlist names, vendor bios) is escaped by context using the framework's auto-escaping template layer instead of a denylist, then stored XSS stops working because the lenient HTML parser can no longer smuggle a payload past string matching.

signal.check: A template uses a raw or unescaped output helper for user-submitted content, or input is filtered with a denylist of blocked strings.

risk.note: None; escaping does not remove legitimate content.

prerequisites: A list of every template that renders user-submitted or stored data
steps: Switch every interpolation to the template engine's auto-escaping syntax.
Grep for raw or unescaped output helpers and justify each remaining one.
For attributes, quote them and escape both quote characters; for src or href, validate the scheme to http and https only.
Never insert user data into comments, tag names, attribute names or element ids.
Spot-check every field with a harmless script payload and confirm it renders as inert text.

test.method: Submit a harmless <script>alert(document.cookie)</script> payload and its encoded variants to every UGC field on staging
test.measure: share of fields where the payload renders as inert text

title: Treat every user-generated field shown to other shoppers as a top-priority XSS target
hypothesis: If product reviews, Q&A, wishlist names and vendor bios are treated as the highest-priority escaping targets, then a stored XSS worm cannot spread through the store the way it once did through unescaped user content on other sites.

signal.check: Reviews, Q&A, wishlist names or vendor bios are not on the priority list for the XSS escaping audit.

risk.note: None; a prioritization decision.

prerequisites: The escaping audit from the context-aware escaping idea
steps: List every field where one shopper's input is shown to another shopper.
Put these fields first in the escaping audit queue.
Re-test these fields specifically after any theme or app change that touches them.

test.method: Re-test UGC fields with a harmless script payload after any related code change
test.measure: share of UGC fields confirmed inert
test.read_point: after each theme or app update touching these fields

does_not_apply_when: A store with no reviews, Q&A, wishlists or vendor bios shown to other shoppers

title: Replace concatenated SQL and shell commands with parameterised queries and argument arrays
hypothesis: If product search, filters and discount-code lookup build queries with parameterised APIs and shell calls use argument arrays instead of string concatenation, then SQL and command injection close on the store's highest-traffic injection surfaces.

signal.check: A query or shell command is built by string concatenation, especially in search, filters or discount-code lookup, and 'we never display query output' is treated as a mitigation.

risk.note: None; parameterisation does not change query results.

prerequisites: A list of every query and shell call built from user input
steps: Submit a single and double quote to every input reaching a query; any database error marks it unsafe.
Convert to parameterised queries using single-statement query APIs.
Convert any shell call to an argument-array API.
For blind cases, test a true and false condition for timing or behavior differences on staging only.
Retest with metacharacters to confirm the whole value is treated as one literal.

test.method: Submit quote and metacharacter test inputs to search, filters and discount lookup on staging
test.measure: count of inputs causing a database error or timing split

title: Add a path or value allow-list to any 'view any file' or report feature
hypothesis: If a file or report generator allow-lists the paths or values it can read instead of relying only on argument-array escaping, then path traversal cannot reach files outside what the feature was meant to expose.

signal.check: A feature that generates a report or serves a file accepts a path or filename parameter with no allow-list check.

risk.note: None; a scope restriction.

prerequisites: A list of file or report features that take a path or filename parameter
steps: List every feature that reads a file or report by a path or filename parameter.
Add an allow-list of valid paths or values for each.
Test with a directory-traversal string (../) and confirm it is rejected.

test.method: Submit a directory-traversal string to each listed feature on staging
test.measure: count of features that reject the traversal string

title: Validate the type of every JSON field before it reaches a type-sensitive backend API
hypothesis: If every JSON field is type-checked before it reaches a buffer constructor, encoder or similar type-sensitive API, then a crafted payload cannot trigger unexpected backend behavior through a type confusion bug.

signal.check: A Node.js or similar backend passes JSON fields directly into buffer constructors or encoders with no type check.

risk.note: None; a validation addition.

prerequisites: A list of endpoints passing JSON fields into type-sensitive APIs
steps: List endpoints that pass JSON input into buffer constructors, encoders or similar APIs.
Add a type check before the value reaches the API.
Reject or coerce any field with an unexpected type.

test.method: Send a JSON field of the wrong type to each listed endpoint
test.measure: share of endpoints that reject the wrong type cleanly

title: Prefer explicit, secure-by-default code and reduce the number of moving parts
hypothesis: If security-relevant code favors explicit logic, secure-by-default APIs and fewer components, then the attack surface shrinks because risk grows with interactions between parts, not just their count.

signal.check: A security-relevant code path has an implicit default, an untested edge case, or more components than the feature needs.

risk.note: Simplification can require regression testing on the affected path.

prerequisites: A code review of the security-relevant path in question
steps: Identify security-relevant code paths with implicit defaults or many components.
Replace implicit logic with explicit checks and fail-fast on impossible states.
Remove or merge components that do not add distinct value.
Treat untested code as presumed broken until covered by a test.

test.method: Count components and implicit defaults on the path before and after simplification
test.measure: count of components and untested branches removed

title: Harden storefront and checkout JavaScript with strict mode, a linter and safe key checks
hypothesis: If storefront and checkout scripts use strict mode, a linter on every commit, strict equality and safe attacker-supplied-key checks, then a class of common JavaScript bugs that attackers rely on gets caught before it ships.

signal.check: Storefront or checkout scripts run without 'use strict', have no linter in the commit pipeline, use loose equality, or index objects with attacker-supplied keys directly.

risk.note: None; a code style and tooling change.

prerequisites: Access to the storefront and checkout JavaScript codebase
steps: Add 'use strict' to storefront and checkout scripts.
Add a linter to the commit pipeline and fix its findings.
Replace loose equality (==) with strict equality (===).
Use Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call for any attacker-supplied key lookup.

test.method: Run the linter against the current codebase and count findings before and after
test.measure: linter findings count

title: Validate the Host header and bind to loopback on any local admin or sync tool
hypothesis: If any local admin, sync or debug tool checks the Host header against an exact expected value and binds to loopback, then DNS rebinding cannot turn a visiting browser into a proxy for that local service.

signal.check: A local HTTP listener (POS helper, print agent, debug port, device UI) checks Origin instead of Host, binds to all interfaces, or exposes a debug port beyond localhost.

risk.note: None; the check only rejects foreign requests.

prerequisites: A list of every HTTP listener on staff machines and LAN devices
steps: List every HTTP listener on staff machines and LAN devices.
Add a first-in-pipeline check: Host header equals the exact expected value, otherwise close the connection.
Bind explicitly to loopback.
Never expose an inspector or debug port beyond localhost.
Test with a raw non-browser client and a bounded rebinding test.

test.method: Send a request with a foreign Host header to each listener
test.measure: whether the foreign-Host request is dropped

does_not_apply_when: No local admin tools, sync helpers, POS helpers or debug ports on staff or store machines

title: Require code review with at least 2 approvers and never edit the live theme
hypothesis: If every theme or app code change goes through version control with at least 2 developer approvals and written standards, then a mistake or malicious change is caught before it reaches the live storefront instead of after.

signal.check: Theme or app code changes go live with no review, or the live theme is edited directly.

risk.note: None; a process change.

prerequisites: Version control for theme and app code
steps: Put theme and app code under version control if not already.
Require at least 2 developer approvals for a significant change.
Write down the review standard so approvals are consistent.
Ban direct edits to the live theme.

test.method: Check the last 10 theme or app changes for a recorded review
test.measure: share of changes with 2 recorded approvals

does_not_apply_when: A solo operator with no second developer available

title: Combine AVS, CVV and 3DS and monitor false declines, not just fraud caught
hypothesis: If AVS, CVV and 3DS are combined instead of relied on individually, and false declines are tracked alongside fraud caught, then the store avoids both under-catching fraud and over-blocking real customers.

signal.check: Only one of AVS, CVV or 3DS is active, or the store tracks fraud caught but not false declines.

risk.note: Changing payment settings can shift real declines; change one at a time.

prerequisites: Order risk, decline and approval rate reports
steps: Confirm which of AVS, CVV and 3DS are active today.
Add tracking for false declines, not only fraud caught.
Review outcomes together monthly, not each control in isolation.

test.method: Compare approval rate, decline rate and confirmed fraud rate for a month
test.measure: false decline rate alongside fraud catch rate

title: Review order risk and decline data before turning on AVS where it is off by default
hypothesis: If order risk reports and decline rates are reviewed before enabling AVS (off by default on Shopify Payments because fraud analysis already covers high-risk orders), then the store avoids trading real sales for a control that may not add much on top of what already runs.

signal.check: AVS is being enabled, or already on, with no before-and-after decline rate comparison.

risk.note: AVS can raise false declines; revert if the decline rate rises unexplained.

prerequisites: 30 to 90 days of order risk and decline data
steps: Pull the order risk report and count high, medium and low risk orders and the decline rate.
Check whether address-mismatch fraud is showing up that current fraud analysis is missing.
If enabling AVS, plan a decline-rate comparison window before and after.
Revert if declines rise on legitimate-looking orders.

test.method: Compare decline rate for 2 to 4 weeks before and after the AVS change
test.measure: decline rate and false-decline complaints

title: Enable dynamic 3D Secure on higher-risk transactions and track approval rate after
hypothesis: If dynamic 3D Secure is turned on for higher-risk transactions and approval rate is tracked before and after, then completed 3DS authentications shift fraudulent chargeback liability to the issuer without the store flying blind on conversion impact.

signal.check: 3DS is off, or on with no tracked approval-rate comparison, on a gateway that supports 3DS 2.0.

risk.note: 3DS adds a step-up factor that can add friction; monitor conversion after enabling.

prerequisites: Gateway support for 3DS 2.0 confirmed
steps: Confirm the gateway supports 3DS 2.0.
Enable dynamic 3DS for higher-risk transactions.
Track approval rate and false declines for 2 to 4 weeks after.
Note the liability shift condition for the relevant card networks.

test.method: Compare approval rate and checkout conversion for 2 to 4 weeks before and after
test.measure: approval rate and cvr_checkout_to_order

title: Wire order-risk ratings to automated capture, review, notify and cancel with a human path
hypothesis: If low, medium and high risk orders are automatically auto-captured, notified or queued for review, with cancel actions limited to specific logged patterns, then card-testing-speed fraud gets handled without manual review of every order or an unreviewed cancel rule blocking a legitimate high-value customer.

signal.check: Every order gets manually reviewed regardless of risk rating, or a cancel rule runs with no human path and no log.

risk.note: A misconfigured cancel rule can auto-cancel a legitimate order; keep a human escalation path.

prerequisites: Shopify Flow or an equivalent automation tool
steps: Start from a fraud automation template in Flow or the gateway's equivalent.
Set low risk to auto-capture, high risk to a review queue, medium risk to notify a reviewer.
Limit cancel actions to specific logged patterns; log every cancel.
Name a human reviewer and a response time for the queue.
Revisit the rule set each quarter and before peak season.

test.method: Send a test high-risk order through and confirm it lands in the review queue, not auto-cancelled
test.measure: whether a test high-value order is wrongly auto-cancelled

title: Detect card-testing bursts by clustering small orders, new accounts and geography mismatch
hypothesis: If the store watches for clusters of small orders, new accounts, IP-to-billing geography mismatch, one BIN range or failed gift card validations, then a card-testing burst gets caught and tightened against before it turns into full fraud and chargebacks.

signal.check: Order and decline logs are not monitored for clustering patterns, and a card-testing burst would only be noticed after chargebacks arrive.

risk.note: Temporary tightening can add friction; roll back after the burst passes.

prerequisites: Order and decline logs with BIN range, account age and IP geography
steps: Confirm the pattern: burst of small orders, new accounts, IP and billing geography mismatch, one BIN range, failed gift card validations.
Temporarily require CVV, hold medium and high risk orders, and rate-limit checkout attempts per IP and account.
Notify the processor and use its fraud tools; void or refund confirmed test authorizations.
Roll back the temporary rules after the burst stops and write up what worked.

test.method: Watch order clustering metrics daily and confirm the burst stops after temporary rules apply
test.measure: small-order cluster rate and chargeback count during and after the burst
test.read_point: during the burst and 2 weeks after

title: Set an internal chargeback alert well below the processor's real flag threshold
hypothesis: If the store confirms its processor's real chargeback programme numbers and sets an internal alert well below them, then the team gets warned in time to act before card acceptance is put at risk.

signal.check: No internal chargeback alert exists, or the store relies on generic industry figures (0.9% flag, 1% stop) instead of its own processor's confirmed numbers.

risk.note: None; a monitoring and alerting change.

prerequisites: The processor's written chargeback programme definition, period and denominator
steps: Ask the processor in writing for its current chargeback programme thresholds, period and denominator.
Set an internal alert at a level clearly below the processor's flag point.
Route the alert to a named person who can act on it.

test.method: Confirm the internal alert fires in a test or against last quarter's data
test.measure: chargeback rate versus the internal alert level

title: Confirm eligibility for a guaranteed chargeback coverage program before relying on it
hypothesis: If eligibility for a program like Shopify Protect is checked and recorded instead of assumed, then the store does not discover mid-dispute that coverage never applied to it, since these programs are not a universal guarantee.

signal.check: The store assumes chargeback coverage from a platform program with no recorded eligibility check.

risk.note: Confirmation only.

prerequisites: Current Shopify Payments and region details
steps: Check current eligibility criteria for the coverage program (for example Shopify Protect: Shopify Payments, US only).
Record whether the store is currently eligible.
Do not present the coverage as guaranteed to the founder or in a client report.

test.method: Confirm eligibility status directly in the payment settings
test.measure: eligibility confirmed yes or no, on file
test.read_point: before relying on it in a business case

title: Add a machine-learning fraud app only after built-in fraud analysis and card-testing response are in place
hypothesis: If a paid ML fraud app is added only after the built-in fraud analysis and card-testing response are already running, then the store avoids paying for a layered tool before the free foundation is even working, and can judge the app's real added value.

signal.check: A paid fraud app is being considered or already running before the platform's own fraud analysis and card-testing response are confirmed working.

risk.note: None; a sequencing decision before spend.

prerequisites: Built-in fraud analysis and card-testing response already running
steps: Confirm built-in fraud analysis (rule 74) and card-testing response (rule 76) are active first.
Review the app's requested permissions before installing.
Measure the app's added catch rate against its cost after a trial period.

test.method: Compare fraud caught and false declines for a month with and without the app
test.measure: incremental fraud caught per dollar of app cost

does_not_apply_when: A store already running built-in fraud analysis and card-testing response with a proven remaining gap

title: Keep malware detection and order-fraud scoring as two separate tools and signals
hypothesis: If malware or endpoint detection results are never treated as an order fraud verdict, then order review decisions stay based on actual fraud signals instead of an unrelated security tool's output.

signal.check: An order review process uses antivirus or malware detection output as a factor in deciding whether an order is fraudulent.

risk.note: None; a process clarification.

prerequisites: Documentation of the order review process
steps: Check whether malware or endpoint detection output feeds into order fraud decisions.
Separate the two signals in the review process documentation.
Retrain reviewers on the distinction.

test.method: Review 10 recent flagged orders for whether malware detection was used as a fraud signal
test.measure: count of orders wrongly using malware detection as a fraud signal
test.read_point: at the next review process audit

title: Keep an evidence trail for every order to answer disputes
hypothesis: If order logs, consent records and delivery proof are retained per order, then chargeback and dispute cases can be answered with evidence instead of accepted by default for lack of a paper trail.

signal.check: A dispute case has no retrievable order log, consent record or delivery proof attached.

risk.note: None; a record-keeping practice.

prerequisites: Order, consent and delivery tracking systems
steps: Confirm order confirmation, consent records and delivery proof are retained per order.
Build a quick-retrieval process for these records when a dispute arrives.
Track dispute win rate by reason code.

test.method: Pull evidence for the last 5 disputed orders and time how long it takes
test.measure: time to retrieve evidence and dispute win rate
test.read_point: after the next disputes are resolved

title: Cap uses per discount code and per customer, and expire a leaked code fast
hypothesis: If every discount code has a use cap per code and per customer and a leaked code is expired quickly, then promo abuse losses drop because a shared or scraped code stops paying out the moment it is spotted.

signal.check: A discount code has no use cap, or redemption for a code spikes with no review, similar to a card-testing cluster.

risk.note: None; caps and expiry are configuration changes.

prerequisites: Access to the discount code system
steps: Set a use cap per code and per customer on every discount code.
Watch redemption spikes the same way as card-testing clusters.
Expire a code fast once it is confirmed leaked or shared publicly.

test.method: Compare redemption patterns before and after caps are added
test.measure: promo code abuse rate

title: Build a friendly-fraud evidence packet for every disputed charge
hypothesis: If every disputed charge gets an evidence packet (order confirmation, delivery proof, IP and device match, order history) instead of an automatic refund, then friendly-fraud losses drop because disputes are contested with real evidence.

signal.check: A customer dispute on a real charge is refunded automatically with no evidence packet built and no dispute win rate tracked.

risk.note: Contesting a real customer's dispute can hurt goodwill; use judgment on repeat-good customers.

prerequisites: The evidence trail from the dispute evidence retention idea
steps: Build a standard evidence packet template: order confirmation, delivery proof, IP and device match, order history.
Fill the packet for every disputed charge before deciding to accept or contest.
Track dispute win rate by reason code to judge whether representment is worth the effort.

test.method: Track dispute win rate for 90 days with the evidence packet in place
test.measure: dispute win rate

title: Re-run the four-pillar security audit when launching a subscription or new payment method
hypothesis: If the four-pillar audit is re-run whenever a subscription or a new payment method launches, then new fraud paths specific to recurring billing get caught before they scale, instead of being covered only by the general annual review.

signal.check: A subscription or new payment method launched with no re-run of the four-pillar audit.

risk.note: Documentation only.

prerequisites: The four-pillar audit already in place
steps: Add a launch checklist item: re-run the four-pillar audit before a new subscription or payment method goes live.
Cover the new payment path specifically for fraud and access controls.
File the updated audit with the launch record.

test.method: Check whether the audit was re-run for the next subscription or payment launch
test.measure: audit completed before launch, yes or no

title: Set up dunning logic that tells an expired-card renewal failure apart from fraud
hypothesis: If a subscription's failed renewal is checked against dunning reasons (expired card, insufficient funds) before being treated as fraud, then genuine subscribers are not wrongly flagged, cancelled or blocked over a card that simply expired.

signal.check: Failed subscription renewals are handled the same way as a fraud decline, with no separate dunning flow for expired or insufficient-funds cards.

risk.note: None; this separates two decision paths that were merged.

prerequisites: Subscription billing platform with decline reason codes
steps: Pull decline reason codes for failed renewals over the last quarter.
Build a separate dunning flow for expired-card and insufficient-funds declines (retry, card update prompt).
Route only genuinely suspicious declines (new card, geography mismatch) to fraud review.
Track how many subscribers were wrongly flagged before the split.

test.method: Compare subscriber churn from wrongly flagged renewals before and after the split
test.measure: subscription_churn from payment-related cancellations

title: Require 2FA with passkeys on every admin and staff account with no exceptions
hypothesis: If 2FA (with passkeys where offered) is required on every admin and staff account including the owner, then account takeover risk drops sharply because this is the cheapest, highest-leverage control a store can apply.

signal.check: Any staff or admin account, including the owner's, has 2FA off.

risk.note: A lost second factor can lock someone out; register a backup factor first.

prerequisites: Access to Settings > Users and permissions or the platform equivalent
steps: List every staff and admin account, including the owner.
Enable 2FA on every account with no exceptions.
Add passkeys where the platform offers them.
Register a second authenticator per admin to avoid lockout.

test.method: Export the staff roster and check 2FA status on each account
test.measure: share of admin accounts with 2FA on

title: Rank second factors and enroll admins on hardware or passkey authenticators first
hypothesis: If second factors are ranked hardware/passkey above TOTP above push above SMS, and admins are enrolled on the strongest option the platform allows, then account takeover from SMS relay or carrier takeover drops because the weakest common factor is no longer the default for the most sensitive accounts.

signal.check: Admin accounts use SMS as their only second factor when a stronger option is available.

risk.note: Hardware keys can be lost; pair with a decided recovery path.

prerequisites: Platform support for WebAuthn or passkeys confirmed
steps: Confirm which second factors the platform supports: hardware/passkey, TOTP, push, SMS.
Enroll owner and full-access accounts on hardware or platform authenticators first.
Use TOTP as fallback; reserve SMS only where nothing else is available.
Record the factor type per account in the access matrix.

test.method: Review the access matrix for factor type per admin account
test.measure: share of admins on hardware or passkey factors

title: Decide the account recovery path before enforcing strong second factors
hypothesis: If the recovery path (backup codes, second hardware key, or an identity-checked admin reset) is decided before rolling out strong MFA, then the store avoids ending up with security only as strong as an unplanned, weak fallback like an SMS reset.

signal.check: MFA is enforced with no documented recovery path, or the fallback is a weaker method than the primary factor (like SMS reset for a hardware-key account).

risk.note: None; a planning step before enforcement.

prerequisites: The 2FA rollout plan
steps: Decide the fallback: backup codes, a second hardware key, or admin reset with an identity check.
Decide explicitly whether SMS fallback for admins is acceptable (recommendation: no).
Document the decision before enforcing MFA broadly.
Keep sealed backup codes offline, never in a repo or chat.

test.method: Simulate a lost-factor scenario and confirm the documented recovery path works
test.measure: whether the recovery path was tested successfully
test.read_point: before the MFA rollout goes live

title: Remove knowledge-based security questions and images as authentication factors
hypothesis: If security questions and anti-phishing security images are removed as authentication factors, then accounts stop relying on a control that a cited study found 72% of users ignored anyway.

signal.check: A login, recovery or step-up flow still uses a knowledge-based security question or an anti-phishing security image.

risk.note: Removing a fallback factor requires a replacement recovery path first.

prerequisites: A decided recovery path to replace the removed factor
steps: Find every place security questions or security images are used.
Replace with a stronger factor or a supported recovery flow.
Remove the weak factor once the replacement is live.

test.method: Confirm no login or recovery flow still offers a security question or image
test.measure: count of flows still using the weak factor

title: Map every staff role to only the admin areas it needs and revoke access outside it
hypothesis: If every staff role (fulfilment, content, marketing, developer, finance, agency) is mapped to only the admin areas it touches, then a compromised or careless account has a much smaller blast radius than broad, convenience-based access.

signal.check: A staff account has full-access permissions granted for convenience with no role-based justification.

risk.note: Over-restricting can block a legitimate task; keep a fast re-grant process.

prerequisites: A current staff and contractor roster with permissions
steps: Map each role to the admin areas it needs.
Grant only those areas per account.
Time-box contractor and agency access with an end date.
Revoke access immediately on departure or role change.
Audit the mapping quarterly.

test.method: Compare each account's actual permissions to its role map
test.measure: count of accounts with excess permissions

title: Restrict and alert on admin logins from new locations, devices or times
hypothesis: If admin logins are restricted or alerted on by IP, geography or time where the platform allows it, then a compromised admin credential is caught by an unusual login location instead of going unnoticed.

signal.check: No alert or restriction exists for an admin login from a new location, device or unusual time, and the plan supports one.

risk.note: None where the platform natively supports this; check plan support first.

prerequisites: Confirmation of what the platform or plan supports for login restriction and alerting
steps: Check what the plan supports for IP allow-listing, geographic or time restriction.
Turn on alerts for admin logins from new locations or devices.
Review admin login locations regularly.

test.method: Trigger a test login from an unfamiliar location or device and confirm the alert fires
test.measure: whether the alert fires on an unfamiliar login

title: Set a password policy of long and unique, breach-checked, and no forced calendar rotation
hypothesis: If the password policy requires length over composition rules, checks against breach lists at signup and change, and rotates only on suspected compromise instead of a calendar, then password strength improves without the rotation fatigue that pushes people toward weaker, reused passwords.

signal.check: The password policy forces calendar rotation (every 60 to 90 days) or composition rules, with no breach-list check.

risk.note: Removing forced rotation is a deliberate, NIST-aligned choice; document it if a client insists on rotation instead.

prerequisites: Access to the password policy settings, or a custom login system
steps: Set minimum length to allow up to 64 characters, with 8 as a bare minimum, and drop composition rules.
Check candidate passwords against a breach list (HIBP-style) at signup and change.
Remove forced calendar rotation; rotate only on suspected or confirmed compromise.
Keep staff accounts strict and MFA-backed; keep guest checkout accounts frictionless but breach-checked.

test.method: Attempt to set a breached password and a 100-character password and confirm the expected result
test.measure: breach-list rejection working; long password accepted

title: Hash any custom-login password with a maintained adaptive hasher and a per-user salt
hypothesis: If passwords are stored only with a maintained adaptive hasher like bcrypt, a per-user salt of 16 to 32 bytes, and pre-hashing for long or Unicode input, then a database leak does not hand out crackable passwords the way a fast hash would.

signal.check: A custom login stores passwords with a fast hash, no per-user salt, or truncates long passwords silently.

risk.note: Changing the hash algorithm requires rehashing on next successful login, not a one-time migration.

prerequisites: A custom login system
steps: Pre-hash if length or Unicode may exceed bcrypt's 72-byte cap.
Hash with bcrypt or an equivalent maintained adaptive hasher at an adjustable work factor.
Store only the returned hash string, with a per-user salt of 16 to 32 bytes.
Grep logs for credential fields on login, signup and reset and redact.
Rehash on next successful login when changing algorithm or cost.

test.method: Round-trip a 100-character or emoji password and confirm correct verification
test.measure: password round-trip success and hash algorithm confirmed

title: Store custom-login usernames uniquely case-insensitive and display in chosen case
hypothesis: If usernames are stored uniquely on a case-insensitive basis but displayed in the user's chosen case, then account confusion and duplicate-account edge cases close without breaking how users expect to see their own name.

signal.check: A custom login allows two accounts to register with the same username differing only in case.

risk.note: None; a uniqueness constraint fix.

prerequisites: A custom login system with username registration
steps: Add a case-insensitive uniqueness constraint on username at signup.
Store the display case as the user typed it.
Test that two case-variant signups of the same username are rejected.

test.method: Attempt to register the same username in two different cases
test.measure: whether the second registration is rejected

title: Rate-limit login, signup and reset per username and per IP, sized from the store's own peak
hypothesis: If login, signup and reset are rate-limited per username and per IP, with the threshold set from the store's own peak legitimate traffic instead of a generic number, then automated guessing is slowed without blocking real customers during a drop or flash sale.

signal.check: Login, signup or reset endpoints have no rate limit, or the limit was never checked against the store's own peak traffic (a drop, flash sale or shared office IP).

risk.note: A threshold set too low can block real customers during a sale; size it from the store's own peak.

prerequisites: Login attempt logs covering at least one peak traffic event
steps: Pull login attempt logs covering the store's highest legitimate traffic peak.
Set the rate limit at about 10 times that peak per username and per IP.
Return a delay or explicit rate-limit error, never a different response by guess correctness.
Raise the threshold if real users get blocked.

test.method: Run scripted repeated login failures against staging and confirm the limit engages without blocking a simulated peak-traffic user
test.measure: scripted failure rate slowed; real-peak simulation unaffected

title: Return identical error messages and timing for wrong password vs no such user everywhere
hypothesis: If login, reset and signup return the same message, status code and timing whether an account exists or not, and guest checkout lookup and loyalty login get the same treatment, then attackers cannot harvest which emails are customers.

signal.check: Login, reset, signup, guest checkout lookup or loyalty login return a different message or respond at a different speed depending on whether the account exists.

risk.note: None unless enumeration risk is judged low enough to trade for a usability improvement.

prerequisites: Access to login, reset, signup, guest checkout and loyalty login flows
steps: Check guest checkout email lookup and loyalty account login specifically, the two most likely leaks.
Return one generic message and status code for missing user, wrong password and disabled account.
Do equal computational work on both paths to close the timing channel.

test.method: Time and compare responses for an existing vs non-existing account on each flow
test.measure: response message, code and timing difference across flows

title: Trigger step-up authentication on new device, new country or many accounts from one source
hypothesis: If a second factor is required on a new device, a new country, a listed suspicious IP, or many accounts tried from one source quickly, then account takeover from a stolen password is caught at the login moment instead of after the fact.

signal.check: A login from a new device, new country or a burst of account attempts from one source does not trigger a step-up challenge.

risk.note: None if admin authentication is never weakened to make step-up easier.

prerequisites: A recognized-device or IP-history tracking mechanism
steps: Add step-up triggers: new device, new IP or country, listed suspicious IP, about 10 accounts from one source in a minute.
Add store-specific triggers: changing a shipping address, adding a payment method, editing payout details.
Never weaken admin authentication to make step-up more convenient.

test.method: Simulate a login from a new device or country and confirm the step-up challenge fires
test.measure: whether the step-up challenge triggers correctly

title: Require re-authentication before changing email, password, payment method or payout details
hypothesis: If sensitive account changes (email, password, payment method, API key, staff, payout details) require re-entering a credential or factor, then a hijacked but still-logged-in session cannot silently take over the account permanently.

signal.check: A logged-in session can change email, password, payment method or payout details with no re-authentication step.

risk.note: None; adds one confirmation step to sensitive actions.
