prerequisites: A list of sensitive account-change actions
steps: List sensitive actions: email, password, payment method, API key, staff, payout details.
Require re-authentication (password or second factor) immediately before each.
Test that a stale session cannot make the change without re-authenticating.

test.method: Attempt each sensitive change from a logged-in session without re-authenticating
test.measure: whether the change is blocked until re-authentication

title: Put CAPTCHA behind the rate limit and exempt API and verified-agent lanes
hypothesis: If CAPTCHA runs only behind the rate limit for repeat offenders, and API and verified-agent lanes are exempt, then automated abuse still gets slowed without failing legitimate headless agents by design or penalizing privacy-conscious shoppers on every form.

signal.check: CAPTCHA runs on every visit to a form or login instead of only after repeated failures, or it sits in front of verified-agent or API traffic.

risk.note: None; CAPTCHA is a speed bump, not a wall, on either setting.

prerequisites: A rate limit already in place on the relevant endpoint
steps: Move CAPTCHA to trigger only after the rate limit threshold is hit.
Exempt confirmed API and verified-agent traffic from CAPTCHA.
Keep the challenge on gift card balance checks and promo code fields behind the rate limit too, not on ordinary browsing.

test.method: Compare conversion rate on the affected form before and after the CAPTCHA placement change
test.measure: cvr_checkout_to_order and bot block rate

title: Separate authentication from authorization and check permissions on every request
hypothesis: If a session only proves identity and permissions are looked up fresh on every request instead of baked into a token, then a stale or copied token cannot carry more access than the account currently has.

signal.check: A token or session carries permission claims that are not re-checked against the current permission table on each request.

risk.note: None; a permission-check architecture change.

prerequisites: Access to the authorization code path
steps: Identify any place a token or session carries baked-in permission claims.
Move permission checks to a fresh lookup on every request.
Apply the same rule to any custom agent or integration credential.

test.method: Revoke a permission and confirm an existing session immediately loses access
test.measure: whether access is revoked without a new login

title: Issue every automation credential as a revocable, scoped, logged record
hypothesis: If every API key, OAuth token, service account and agent token is scoped to one brand and one task, generated from a secure random source, and logged per action, then a leaked or misused automation credential is fast to find and revoke.

signal.check: An API key or automation credential is shared across brands or tasks, has no expiry or scope, or its use is not logged.

risk.note: None; a credential issuance practice.

prerequisites: An inventory of current API keys and automation credentials
steps: List every current automation credential and what it accesses.
Scope each to one brand and one task; revoke and reissue any broad credential.
Log every use per action.
Confirm each credential can be individually revoked.

test.method: Revoke one credential and confirm only its scoped task is affected
test.measure: whether revocation is scoped correctly

title: Lock or flag customer accounts and force resets after any breach touching the customer base
hypothesis: If affected customer accounts are proactively locked or flagged and forced to reset after any breach the brand is tangentially involved in, then account takeover from the breach's leaked credentials is cut off before it spreads.

signal.check: A breach notice touching the customer base (the brand's own or a third party the brand uses) arrives with no plan to lock, flag or force-reset affected accounts.

risk.note: Forced resets create a support load; communicate why clearly to customers.

prerequisites: A way to identify affected accounts from a breach notice
steps: On any breach notice touching the customer base, identify affected accounts.
Lock or flag those accounts.
Force a password reset and notify affected customers with a clear reason.

test.method: Run a tabletop drill: simulate a breach notice and time the lock/flag/reset response
test.measure: time from notice to accounts locked

title: Run quarterly phishing simulation training covering email, voice and SMS for all staff
hypothesis: If staff get quarterly simulated phishing training covering email, voice and SMS with written protocols for suspicious requests, then phishing-driven account and payment fraud drops because staff recognize and report attempts before acting on them.

signal.check: Staff have never had simulated phishing training, or training was a one-off instead of a recurring quarterly practice.

risk.note: None; a training program.

prerequisites: A list of all staff and their contact channels
steps: Run a simulated phishing test covering email, voice and SMS.
Share written protocols for verifying any payment redirect or credential request through a separate channel.
Tell customers the brand will never ask for personal information by email or text.
Repeat the simulation quarterly and track improvement.

test.method: Track the simulated phishing click rate and report rate each quarter
test.measure: click rate and report rate on the simulated phishing test

title: Design any biometric login so the biometric data never leaves the device
hypothesis: If a biometric login design keeps the biometric data on the device to unlock a local key that then authenticates, instead of sending biometric data anywhere, then a server breach cannot expose customers' fingerprints or face data.

signal.check: A biometric login feature is being designed or built that transmits or stores biometric data off the device.

risk.note: None; a design constraint check before building.

prerequisites: A planned or existing biometric login feature
steps: Confirm the biometric design uses the device's local authenticator (WebAuthn/passkey) rather than sending biometric data to the server.
Reject any vendor or library that requires transmitting raw biometric data.

test.method: Review the biometric feature's data flow diagram for any off-device transmission
test.measure: confirmed on-device-only data flow

does_not_apply_when: A store with no biometric login feature planned

title: Build a bot and agent traffic baseline by agent, endpoint and intent before setting any policy
hypothesis: If the store identifies which agents access the site, at which endpoints, and with what intent (indexing, comparing, extracting) before writing any bot policy, then the policy targets real traffic patterns instead of guesswork.

signal.check: A bot or agent policy exists (or is being planned) with no traffic baseline showing which agents hit which endpoints and why.

risk.note: None; a data-gathering step before policy.

prerequisites: Server or CDN logs covering at least 2 to 4 weeks of traffic
steps: Pull traffic logs and classify by agent identity, endpoint and apparent intent.
Separate human, verified agent, and unverified automation traffic.
Document the baseline before writing any allow, block or challenge rule.

test.method: Compare the written baseline to a fresh traffic pull a month later
test.measure: baseline completeness: agents, endpoints and intent classified

title: Set an enforceable bot policy per endpoint and category instead of one site-wide switch
hypothesis: If bot policy is set per endpoint and agent category (allow, monitor, rate-limit, authenticate or block) with trust tiers, then enforcement actually matches the risk of each surface instead of one blunt setting that either blocks too much or too little.

signal.check: The bot policy is a single site-wide setting instead of a rule per endpoint and category, or the policy cannot be technically enforced.

risk.note: A too-strict rule on a real surface can block legitimate agents; ship as monitor first.

prerequisites: The bot traffic baseline
steps: Define trust tiers for agent categories.
Set a policy (allow, monitor, rate-limit, authenticate or block) per endpoint and category.
Confirm each policy line has an actual enforcement mechanism, not just documentation.
Ship any new restriction as monitor-only first, then challenge, then block.

test.method: Test each endpoint's policy against a sample of real traffic from each category
test.measure: share of policy lines with confirmed enforcement

title: Keep browsing frictionless and put the strictest checks at checkout and account changes
hypothesis: If catalogue browsing stays frictionless while checkout and account modification get the strictest verification, then the store loses less legitimate browsing and agent-driven traffic while still protecting the points where fraud actually pays off.

signal.check: Verification friction (CAPTCHA, challenges) appears on browsing pages while checkout or account-change endpoints have lighter checks.

risk.note: None; a friction reallocation, not a new control.

prerequisites: The per-endpoint bot policy
steps: Audit where friction (CAPTCHA, challenges, verification) currently sits.
Remove or lighten friction on browsing and catalogue pages.
Move the strictest verification to checkout and account modification endpoints.

test.method: Compare browsing-to-cart conversion before and after moving friction
test.measure: cvr_pdp_to_cart

title: Score bot risk in 4 tiers and re-evaluate continuously within a session
hypothesis: If bot and agent risk is scored in 4 tiers (permit, verify, challenge, prevent) and re-evaluated continuously during a session instead of once at entry, then a session that starts as browsing and drifts into scraping or card testing gets stopped mid-session instead of being waved through on its first-entry score.

signal.check: Bot or agent risk is scored once at entry with no re-evaluation as the session continues.

risk.note: Threshold tuning needed; start conservative to avoid over-blocking.

prerequisites: The per-endpoint bot policy and a tool capable of in-session scoring
steps: Define the 4 tiers: permit low-risk browsing, verify on behavioral shift, challenge on financial or account risk, prevent confirmed malicious automation.
Set thresholds from the brand's own traffic baseline, not a vendor default.
Re-evaluate risk continuously within the session, not only at entry.

test.method: Track sessions that shift from browsing to a higher-risk action and confirm they get re-scored
test.measure: share of drifting sessions caught mid-session

title: Default to challenge over block for ambiguous automation; reserve block for confirmed malicious traffic
hypothesis: If ambiguous automated traffic is challenged instead of blocked outright, then the store keeps legitimate agent-driven and human revenue that a blanket-block posture would otherwise lose, while confirmed malicious automation still gets prevented.

signal.check: The current bot rule blocks any traffic that looks automated, with no challenge step in between allow and block.

risk.note: Loosening a block rule can let more bad traffic through temporarily; monitor closely after the change.

prerequisites: The 4-tier risk scoring in place
steps: Identify current block rules that fire on ambiguous, not confirmed-malicious, traffic.
Replace with a challenge step for ambiguous cases.
Reserve outright blocking for traffic confirmed malicious by pattern or behavior.

test.method: Compare legitimate agent and human traffic volume before and after the change
test.measure: ai_referrals and blocked-traffic false-positive rate

title: Pair agent identity credentials with behavior monitoring so a drifting agent is still stopped
hypothesis: If accepted AI shopping agents present an identity credential and their behavior is monitored against declared intent, then a verified agent from a compromised server or one that drifts from browsing to scraping or card testing still gets stopped, instead of being waved through on identity alone.

signal.check: The store accepts agent identity credentials with no behavior monitoring layer checking whether actions still match declared intent.

risk.note: Agent identity protocols are still forming; re-verify vendor and protocol status before committing.

prerequisites: A decision to accept verified shopping agents
steps: Confirm current status of agent identity protocols (Visa TAP, Mastercard Agent Pay, Skyfire KYA, Web Bot Auth) before committing.
Require an identity credential from any agent claiming verified status.
Layer behavior monitoring that checks actions against declared intent, regardless of credential.
Stop an agent immediately if its behavior drifts, even with a valid credential.

test.method: Simulate an agent with a valid credential that starts scraping or card testing and confirm it is stopped
test.measure: whether drifting behavior is caught despite a valid credential

does_not_apply_when: A store not yet accepting any verified AI shopping agent

title: Audit declines for headless-traffic false positives before reading them as fraud
hypothesis: If declines are traced to see whether they cluster on headless or API traffic with no other risk signal, then the store stops misreading a missing-client-side-telemetry rule as fraud when it is really a bot rule built only for browser sessions.

signal.check: Decline reasons are not traced back to whether the traffic was headless or lacked client-side telemetry, and headless legitimate agents may be failing invisible CAPTCHA or fingerprinting checks by design.

risk.note: None; an audit and reporting exercise.

prerequisites: Decline reason logs with traffic-type classification
steps: Pull decline reasons for the last month and classify by traffic type (browser vs headless/API).
Check whether declines cluster on headless traffic with no other risk signal present.
If so, treat it as a misconfigured rule, not fraud, and adjust the rule.

test.method: Re-run the decline audit a month after the rule adjustment
test.measure: false-decline rate on headless traffic

title: Give any accepted shopping agent scoped, per-action authorization, never standing payment access
hypothesis: If an accepted AI shopping agent gets each action authorized against merchant policy individually, instead of inheriting broad or standing payment and admin access, then a compromised or misbehaving agent cannot act beyond what a single approved action allows.

signal.check: An accepted agent holds standing payment or admin credentials instead of per-action authorization checked against policy.

risk.note: Rebuilding agent access as per-action can add development effort; scope before broad agent adoption.

prerequisites: A decision to accept an AI shopping agent integration
steps: Design agent access so each action (read catalogue, add to cart, checkout) is authorized separately against merchant policy.
Never grant an agent that only reads the catalogue any payment or admin credential.
Test that an agent action outside its granted scope is rejected.

test.method: Attempt an out-of-scope action (like a payment change) from a catalogue-only agent credential
test.measure: whether the out-of-scope action is rejected

does_not_apply_when: A store not accepting any AI shopping agent integration

title: Treat everything an agent reads as untrusted data, never as an instruction
hypothesis: If product descriptions, reviews, feeds, support messages and tool output are always treated as untrusted data by any agent touching the store, with permissions enforced outside the model, then a crafted piece of content cannot manipulate an agent into an unauthorized action.

signal.check: An in-house or third-party agent (including an ecomOS agent) treats content it reads as instructions, or relies on input filtering alone instead of enforcing permissions outside the model.

risk.note: None; this is an architecture rule for any agent touching the store.

prerequisites: An inventory of every agent that reads storefront content
steps: List every agent (in-house or third-party) that reads product descriptions, reviews, feeds, support messages or tool output.
Enforce permissions and business rules outside the model, not through input filtering alone.
Test with a crafted piece of content designed to look like an instruction and confirm it is ignored as an instruction.

test.method: Plant a test instruction inside a review or feed and confirm the agent does not act on it
test.measure: whether the planted instruction is followed or ignored
test.read_point: before any new agent goes live

title: Design multi-agent workflows against the 5 known failure modes
hypothesis: If any multi-agent workflow is checked against trust asymmetry, partial context, distributed attack, instruction drift and runaway delegation, then the store avoids the specific ways agent chains fail even though these are academic scenarios rather than confirmed incidents.

signal.check: A multi-agent workflow is planned or live with no check against these 5 failure modes.

risk.note: None; a design review checklist.

prerequisites: A documented multi-agent workflow
steps: List each hop in the workflow and who relays what to whom.
Check for trust asymmetry: does a hop act on a relayed instruction without checking its source.
Check for partial context, distributed attack across sites, instruction drift through re-summarizing, and runaway delegation loops.
Add a check or limit for each failure mode found.

test.method: Run a tabletop walkthrough of the workflow against each failure mode
test.measure: count of failure modes with a documented mitigation

does_not_apply_when: A store with no multi-agent workflow in use or planned

title: Run continuous API discovery and flag which endpoints expose sensitive data
hypothesis: If API discovery runs continuously instead of once, and every endpoint is flagged for whether it exposes sensitive data, then undocumented or forgotten APIs stop being the store's biggest unknown attack surface.

signal.check: No current API inventory exists, or a store discovery has never flagged which endpoints expose sensitive data.

risk.note: None; a discovery and tagging exercise.

prerequisites: Access to run an API discovery scan or manual review
steps: Run a discovery pass across all known and suspected endpoints, including undocumented ones.
Flag each endpoint for whether it exposes sensitive data.
Set discovery to run on a recurring schedule, not as a one-off.

test.method: Compare 2 discovery passes a quarter apart for newly found endpoints
test.measure: count of previously unknown endpoints found

title: Retest login, checkout and webhook flows end to end after every WAF or bot rule change
hypothesis: If login, checkout and webhook traffic are retested end to end after every WAF or bot rule change, then a false positive that blocks a real order gets caught before it costs sales, instead of surfacing as a mystery drop in conversion.

signal.check: A WAF or bot rule changed with no retest of login, checkout or webhook flows afterward.

risk.note: None; a testing discipline.

prerequisites: A basic end-to-end test script for login, checkout and webhook delivery
steps: Build or maintain a simple end-to-end test for login, checkout and webhook delivery.
Run it immediately after any WAF or bot rule change.
Roll back the rule if any of the 3 flows breaks.

test.method: Run the end-to-end test suite right after each rule change
test.measure: pass or fail on login, checkout and webhook flows

title: Stop using User-Agent as an access control; treat it only as a weak coarse signal
hypothesis: If User-Agent is used only for coarse blocking of a self-identified abusive tool and never as an access control, then bypassing security by simply changing the User-Agent string stops working as an attack path.

signal.check: A rule grants or denies access based on User-Agent string matching, treating it as a trustworthy identity signal.

risk.note: None; a downgrade of an unreliable signal.

prerequisites: A review of current access rules referencing User-Agent
steps: Find every rule that grants or denies access based on User-Agent.
Replace access-control use with a real check (Origin, session, credential).
Keep User-Agent only for coarse blocking of tools that self-identify as abusive.

test.method: Change the User-Agent string on a request and confirm access rules do not change based on it alone
test.measure: count of access rules still keyed on User-Agent

title: Investigate combined bot indicators before blocking, not any single signal alone
hypothesis: If unusual traffic spikes, failed gift card validations, repeated failed logins, abandoned cart reservations and price scraping patterns are reviewed together, then a genuine bot pattern is confirmed before a block ships, instead of reacting to one noisy signal alone.

signal.check: A block decision is made from a single indicator (like a traffic spike) with no cross-check against the other bot indicators.

risk.note: None; an investigation discipline before acting.

prerequisites: Monitoring for traffic, gift card validation, login failures, cart reservations and scraping
steps: Pull all 5 indicators together for the suspicious window: traffic spikes, gift card failures, login failures, abandoned reservations, scraping patterns.
Confirm at least 2 indicators agree before treating it as a confirmed bot pattern.
Investigate root cause before writing a permanent block rule.

test.method: Review the last flagged incident for how many indicators were checked before the block
test.measure: count of indicators cross-checked before action

title: Red-team only the store's own systems, on a recurring cadence, after the bot policy ships
hypothesis: If red-team testing is run only against systems the store owns and is authorized to test, on a recurring cadence after the bot policy is live, then real gaps in the deployed policy get found by the store first, safely and legally.

signal.check: No red-team testing has been run against the store's own bot and fraud defenses since they went live, or testing has targeted systems the store does not own.

risk.note: Test only owned systems with written authorization to avoid legal exposure.

prerequisites: The bot and agent policy already live
steps: Confirm testing scope covers only systems the store owns and is authorized to test.
Run a red-team pass against the live bot and fraud defenses.
Set a recurring cadence for repeat testing.
Feed findings back into the policy.

test.method: Review red-team findings and confirm each led to a policy or control change
test.measure: count of findings actioned

does_not_apply_when: A store with no bot or agent policy live yet to test

title: Watch for reseller and scalper bots by tracking one payment method across many accounts during a drop
hypothesis: If one shipping address or payment method spread across many accounts, plus purchase velocity per SKU, is tracked during a drop, then reseller and scalper bots that complete checkout and resell at markup get caught, unlike hoarding bots that just abandon carts.

signal.check: Purchase velocity per SKU and shared payment method or address across accounts are not tracked during a drop.

risk.note: A false match can flag a real repeat customer or shared household card; review before blocking.

prerequisites: Order data with shipping address, payment method and account id for drop windows
steps: Pull orders from the last drop and check for one address or payment method spread across many accounts.
Track purchase velocity per SKU during the drop window.
Flag matches for review before the next drop ships.

test.method: Compare flagged reseller patterns across 2 drops, one with monitoring and one without
test.measure: count of confirmed reseller patterns caught

does_not_apply_when: No limited drops or high resale-demand products

title: Review app permissions quarterly and after adding any checkout, payment or customer-data app
hypothesis: If installed app permissions are reviewed quarterly and immediately after any new checkout, payment or customer-data app is added, then permission creep and unused broad access get caught on a schedule instead of drifting for years.

signal.check: No scheduled review of app permissions exists, or a recently installed checkout, payment or customer-data app has not been re-audited.

risk.note: None; a review cadence.

prerequisites: Access to Settings > Apps and sales channels or the platform equivalent
steps: Export the installed app list with permissions.
Remove unused apps; confirm permissions match function for kept apps.
Prefer Built for Shopify status and a review score above 3.75 as a heuristic, not a guarantee.
Re-audit immediately after any new checkout, payment or customer-data app is added.

test.method: Compare the app list and permissions to the last quarter's audit
test.measure: count of apps with excess permissions found and removed

title: Keep a live inventory of every app, theme, plugin and dependency with owner and last use
hypothesis: If every app, theme, plugin and dependency is tracked with owner, version, permissions, last use and current maintainer, then trust established at install time gets re-checked as maintainers change, instead of assumed to hold forever.

signal.check: No single inventory lists every app, theme, plugin and dependency with an owner and last-use date.

risk.note: None; an inventory exercise.

prerequisites: Access to app, theme and dependency lists
steps: Build one inventory listing every app, theme, plugin and dependency.
Record owner, version, permissions, last use and current maintainer for each.
Update the inventory whenever something is added, removed or its maintainer changes.

test.method: Spot-check 5 entries against the live store for accuracy
test.measure: share of inventory entries confirmed accurate

title: Lock dependency versions, review new direct dependencies, and check names for typosquats
hypothesis: If dependency versions are locked, every new direct dependency is reviewed, and package names are checked against typosquats, then a malicious or compromised package is far less likely to slip into the codebase unnoticed.

signal.check: Lockfiles are not diffed on change, a new dependency was added with no review, or package names have never been checked for typosquats.

risk.note: None; a review discipline on top of existing dependency management.

prerequisites: A lockfile-based dependency management setup
steps: Diff the lockfile since the last audit.
Review every new direct dependency before merging.
Check package names against common typosquat patterns.
Confirm the published artifact matches the source repository for critical packages.

test.method: Run the typosquat and lockfile diff check on the next dependency update
test.measure: count of suspicious dependencies found

title: Run installs only in a disposable, network-restricted build environment
hypothesis: If npm install and equivalents run only in a disposable, network-restricted build environment that then promotes the built artifact, then a malicious install script cannot reach production credentials or persist on a host that is torn down after each build.

signal.check: Dependency installs run directly on a production or long-lived host instead of a disposable build environment.

risk.note: None; a build pipeline change.

prerequisites: A CI/CD pipeline or equivalent build system
steps: Confirm where installs currently run.
Move installs to a disposable, network-restricted build environment.
Promote only the built artifact to production, never the build host itself.

test.method: Confirm the production host never runs an install command directly
test.measure: install location confirmed disposable and isolated

title: Read changelogs before updating and subscribe to platform and app security bulletins
hypothesis: If changelogs are read before updating and the store subscribes to platform and app security bulletins, then updates stop being blind and a disclosed vulnerability in a used app or dependency gets noticed and patched fast.

signal.check: Updates are applied with no changelog review, or the store has no subscription to platform or app security bulletins.

risk.note: None; a subscription and reading habit.

prerequisites: A list of the store's main apps and dependencies
steps: Subscribe to security bulletins for the platform and every major app or dependency.
Read the changelog before applying any update.
Enable automatic security updates where safe to do so.

test.method: Check whether the last 3 updates had a changelog reviewed beforehand
test.measure: share of updates with a documented changelog review

title: Audit browser extensions on every admin, fulfilment and support machine
hypothesis: If browser extensions are audited on admin, fulfilment and support machines, not just admin machines, then a popular extension that later gets sold and turns malicious is caught wherever it sits, since fulfilment and support staff handle live order and payment-route data daily too.

signal.check: Browser extensions are audited on admin machines only, or not audited at all, while fulfilment and support machines are untouched.

risk.note: None; an inventory and removal exercise.

prerequisites: Access to list installed browser extensions on staff machines
steps: List installed browser extensions on admin, fulfilment and support machines.
Remove any extension with no known, justified purpose.
Add extensions to the standing app inventory for ongoing tracking.

test.method: Re-check extensions on a sample of machines after the audit
test.measure: count of unknown extensions removed
test.read_point: right after the audit, then quarterly

title: Rescore every disclosed vulnerability against the brand's own deployment
hypothesis: If a disclosed CVE is rescored for the brand's own deployment instead of taken at its vendor-given severity, then triage effort goes to what actually threatens this store instead of following a generic score that may not apply.

signal.check: Disclosed vulnerabilities are triaged using only the vendor's CVSS score with no rescoring for the brand's actual exposure.

risk.note: None; a triage practice.

prerequisites: A process for receiving disclosed vulnerabilities
steps: Use CVE, CWE and CVSS as shared vocabulary for the finding.
Rescore severity based on whether the brand's own deployment actually uses the affected code path.
Prioritize fixes by the rescored severity, not the vendor default.

test.method: Compare vendor severity to the brand's rescored severity on the next 5 disclosed vulnerabilities
test.measure: count of findings rescored differently from vendor default

title: Publish a vulnerability disclosure channel with a stated response and fix SLA
hypothesis: If the store publishes an intake channel for security researchers with a stated response time (about 24 hours) and update cadence (about 48 hours), then a real vulnerability gets reported responsibly instead of disclosed publicly or exploited first.

signal.check: No public channel exists for a security researcher to report a finding, or no response SLA is stated.

expected_effect.size: target about 24 hours first response, 48 hours update

risk.note: None; a channel and process to publish.

prerequisites: A monitored email address or a platform like a disclosure program page
steps: Publish an intake channel (a security email or a disclosure platform).
Commit to a response time (about 24 hours) and an update cadence (about 48 hours), faster for high severity.
Set an embargo that binds the team and any contractor until the fix ships.
Publish the fix and its severity once resolved.

test.method: Send a test report to the channel and time the response
test.measure: time to first response
test.read_point: right after publishing the channel, then on each real report

does_not_apply_when: A store with no custom code or public-facing app

title: Threat-model the hosting model itself, not just the application code
hypothesis: If the threat model covers the hosting model (dangling DNS, cloud misconfiguration, serverless cost exhaustion) alongside the application code, then infrastructure-level risks get caught instead of being invisible to a code-only review.

signal.check: The store's threat model covers application code but has no row for dangling DNS, cloud misconfiguration or serverless cost exhaustion.

risk.note: None; a documentation addition to the threat model.

prerequisites: The hosting model documented: shared VM, serverless or hosted platform
steps: Add a hosting-model row to the threat model.
Check for dangling DNS, cloud misconfiguration and, if serverless, cost-exhaustion exposure.
Name an owner and a control for each hosting-model risk found.

test.method: Review the updated threat model for hosting-model coverage
test.measure: hosting-model risks documented with an owner
test.read_point: at the next threat model refresh

title: Run daily versioned backups to 3 separated locations with one ransomware-safe copy, tested for restore
hypothesis: If backups run daily, are versioned, kept in at least 3 geographically separate locations with one ransomware-protected copy, and are restore-tested on a schedule, then the store can actually recover from a ransomware or data-loss event instead of discovering the backup never worked.

signal.check: Backups exist but have never been restore-tested, there is only one copy, or no copy is protected from ransomware.

risk.note: None; backup infrastructure only, no live-store change.

prerequisites: Definition of critical data: products, orders, customers, content, theme code, configuration, Flow rules
steps: Define what counts as critical data for the store.
Automate daily versioned backups to at least 3 geographically separate locations.
Protect at least one copy from ransomware (immutable or offline).
Run a restore to a test store or staging and time it.
Set a restore-test cadence, since no source gives one (quarterly is a reasonable placeholder).

test.method: Run a full restore and check the restored data against a checksum or count
test.measure: restore success and time to complete

title: Log admin, order-risk, Flow and DNS or header changes, with someone assigned to act
hypothesis: If admin logins, order-risk outcomes, Flow actions, app installs and DNS or header changes are logged with a named person assigned to act, then alerts actually get read and acted on instead of accumulating unread.

signal.check: Logging exists for some of these events but no one is assigned to review or act on the alerts.

risk.note: None; a logging and ownership assignment.

prerequisites: Logging capability across the listed event types
steps: Confirm logging exists for admin logins, order-risk outcomes, Flow actions, app installs, DNS and header changes, and automation credential use.
Assign a named person to review alerts on a set cadence.
Test that a real alert reaches that person and gets acted on.

test.method: Send a test alert and time how long until the assigned person acts
test.measure: time from alert to acknowledged action

title: Scan storefront files for malware on a schedule and treat any detection as a breach until proven otherwise
hypothesis: If storefront files are scanned for malware on a set schedule with file-change alerts, and any detection is treated as a breach until proven otherwise, then a skimmer or backdoor gets caught fast instead of sitting undetected on the checkout page.

signal.check: No scheduled malware scan exists for storefront files, or a past detection was dismissed without full investigation.

risk.note: None; a scanning schedule.

prerequisites: A malware scanning tool for storefront files, or theme-change monitoring on a hosted platform
steps: Set a scan schedule (daily to monthly) with file-change alerts.
Treat any detection as a confirmed breach until investigation proves otherwise.
On Shopify, monitor theme code changes as the equivalent surface.

test.method: Trigger a test file change and confirm the alert fires
test.measure: whether the test change triggers an alert

does_not_apply_when: A fully hosted-checkout store where theme code changes are the equivalent surface

title: Treat unexplained changes to shipping address, order contents or payment routes as compromise signals
hypothesis: If unexplained changes to shipping addresses, order contents, contact details, payment routes or admin users are treated as compromise signals rather than data entry errors, then account and system compromise is caught at the moment it starts changing real orders and money.

signal.check: A changed shipping address, payment route or new admin user is logged but not automatically flagged for review as a possible compromise signal.

risk.note: None; a monitoring and review rule.

prerequisites: Logging of order, payment route and admin user changes
steps: Flag any change to shipping address, order contents, contact details, payment routes or admin users for review.
Investigate flagged changes as a possible compromise, not a routine data entry issue.
Escalate confirmed compromise into the incident runbook.

test.method: Review the last month's flagged changes for how quickly they were investigated
test.measure: time from flagged change to investigation

title: Follow a fixed sequence when a skimming signal appears: offline, remove, rotate, check, notify
hypothesis: If a skimming or checkout compromise signal triggers a fixed sequence (checkout offline, scripts removed, credentials rotated, admin and payment routes checked, insurance and legal notification), then the incident is contained fast instead of improvised under pressure.

signal.check: No written sequence exists for what to do the moment a skimming signal (unexpected checkout script or file change) appears.

risk.note: Get qualified security and legal help for a real incident; this sequence is an outline, not a full plan.

prerequisites: Written incident runbook access during a live incident
steps: Take the checkout page offline the moment a skimming signal appears.
Inventory and remove every unneeded script; investigate and eliminate the source.
Rotate admin and integration credentials (a human does this, never in chat).
Check for new admin users and changed payment routes.
Check cyber insurance coverage, then notify per legal requirements.

test.method: Run a tabletop drill simulating a skimming signal and time each step
test.measure: time from signal to checkout offline and credentials rotated

title: Confirm GDPR/CCPA exposure by customer location and keep the fine and notification duty visible
hypothesis: If the store confirms which customer locations bring it under GDPR or CCPA and keeps the fine exposure (up to 4% of global revenue) and notification duties visible to the founder, then a breach or complaint does not become a surprise legal event on top of the security incident itself.

signal.check: The store has customers in the EU, UK or California with no documented awareness of GDPR or CCPA duties.

risk.note: This flags exposure; it does not replace legal advice.

prerequisites: A breakdown of customers by region
steps: Confirm whether the store sells to the EU, UK or California.
Document the fine exposure and notification duty for each applicable region.
Make sure the founder has seen this before an incident, not only during one.

test.method: Confirm the founder can state the store's GDPR/CCPA exposure from memory or a written note
test.measure: exposure documented and reviewed by the founder

does_not_apply_when: A store that sells only to regions with no GDPR or CCPA exposure

title: Build the incident runbook to handle chargebacks, fines and churn together, not as separate tracks
hypothesis: If the incident runbook plans for chargebacks, fines and customer churn as one compounding event instead of 3 separate tracks, then the response covers the full cost of an incident instead of handling only the technical piece.

signal.check: The incident runbook covers technical containment but has no plan for the chargeback, fine and churn impact happening at once.

risk.note: None; a runbook completeness check.

prerequisites: An existing incident detection and containment plan
steps: Add a chargeback-handling step to the runbook alongside technical containment.
Add a regulatory notification step with the relevant windows.
Add a customer communication step aimed at limiting churn.
Assign an owner to each of the 3 tracks.

test.method: Run a tabletop drill that includes all 3 tracks, not just technical containment
test.measure: whether all 3 tracks have a named owner and were exercised

title: Read disclosed vulnerabilities in the brand's own stack quarterly and check for the same code shape
hypothesis: If disclosed vulnerabilities in the brand's own technology stack are read quarterly as learning material, then the brand's own code gets checked for the same shape of bug before it is ever exploited there.

signal.check: No one reviews disclosed vulnerabilities in the store's own stack on a schedule.

risk.note: None; a reading and review habit.

prerequisites: A list of the brand's own stack components to watch
steps: List the brand's own stack components (frameworks, libraries, platform).
Read disclosed vulnerabilities for these components quarterly.
Check the brand's own code for the same bug shape.

test.method: Confirm the quarterly review happened and note any matching code found
test.measure: review completed on schedule, yes or no

title: Inventory every third-party tag and script with vendor, purpose and consent status
hypothesis: If every third-party tag, pixel and script is inventoried with its vendor, purpose, what it can observe, and whether it is disclosed and consented, then a tag whose purpose nobody can name gets removed instead of quietly staying on the site.

signal.check: No inventory exists of third-party tags with vendor, purpose and consent status, or a tag on the site cannot be attributed to anyone.

risk.note: Removing a tag with no known purpose can break a feature; confirm before removing.

prerequisites: A crawl of storefront, account and checkout pages
steps: Crawl storefront, account and checkout pages and list every third-party request.
For each, record vendor, purpose, cookies set or read, data observed, and consent category.
Confirm the privacy policy mentions each disclosed use.
Remove any tag with no owner or purpose.

test.method: Recrawl after the inventory and confirm no unowned tag remains
test.measure: count of unowned tags found and removed
test.read_point: right after the inventory, then quarterly

title: Audit ad and analytics tags for fingerprinting and remove any the brand cannot justify
hypothesis: If ad and analytics tags are checked for fingerprinting techniques (canvas, WebGL, audio, fonts, hardware signals) and any the brand cannot justify are removed, then privacy exposure drops on the very tags most likely to carry unjustified fingerprinting: the store's own retargeting and ad pixels.

signal.check: A retargeting or ad pixel on the site uses canvas, WebGL, audio or font fingerprinting with no documented business justification.

risk.note: Removing a fingerprinting technique can reduce some attribution accuracy; weigh against privacy exposure.

prerequisites: The third-party tag inventory
steps: Start the fingerprinting audit with the store's own retargeting and ad pixels.
Check what each tag actually does technically, not just what the vendor claims.
Remove or disable any fingerprinting technique the brand cannot justify.

test.method: Recheck tag behavior after the audit for remaining fingerprinting calls
test.measure: count of unjustified fingerprinting calls removed

title: Re-verify current browser cookie and tracking defaults before building any measurement plan
hypothesis: If current browser cookie and tracking defaults are checked before building a measurement plan, instead of assumed from older documentation, then the plan does not silently break when a browser default has already changed or reversed.

signal.check: A measurement or tracking plan cites a browser default with no recent verification date.

risk.note: None; a verification step.

prerequisites: Access to check current browser vendor documentation
steps: Before building a tracking or measurement plan, check current per-browser cookie and tracking defaults.
Note the verification date next to any default cited in the plan.
Revisit before any plan that depends on cookie behavior ships.

test.method: Check the plan's cited defaults against current browser documentation
test.measure: share of cited defaults with a current verification date

title: Never repurpose HSTS as a tracking mechanism; keep it for security only
hypothesis: If HSTS is kept strictly as a security feature and never repurposed as a tracking supercookie, then the store avoids a privacy exposure that a third party could otherwise exploit through the security header itself.

signal.check: Any code or third-party script uses HSTS state as a tracking or identification signal.

risk.note: None; a purpose-limitation rule.

prerequisites: Access to current HSTS configuration
steps: Check whether any script or vendor is using HSTS state for tracking purposes.
Confirm HSTS configuration is used only for security, not identification.

test.method: Audit code and third-party scripts for any HSTS-based tracking technique
test.measure: count of HSTS-based tracking uses found

title: Publish a specific privacy policy covering AI agent interactions and run a compliant consent banner
hypothesis: If the privacy policy specifically states what is collected, why and how it is stored, addresses AI agent interactions, and the consent banner meets GDPR standards where in scope, then the store's actual privacy posture matches what it claims, instead of a generic template no one has customized.

signal.check: The privacy policy is generic with no specific data collection detail or AI agent mention, or the consent banner fires before consent in the EU or UK.

risk.note: None; a policy and configuration update.

prerequisites: Current data collection practices documented
steps: Write a specific privacy policy: what is collected, why, and how stored.
Add a section addressing AI agent interactions if the store accepts agents.
Confirm the consent banner blocks non-essential tags before consent in the EU and UK.
Verify any automated policy template or Customer Privacy API claim against current documentation.

test.method: Test the consent banner from a fresh EU-located browser profile
test.measure: whether non-essential tags fire before consent
test.read_point: right after the policy and banner update

title: Never reuse a contact detail collected for 2FA or receipts for retargeting without separate consent
hypothesis: If a phone number or email collected for 2FA, receipts or order status is never silently reused for ad retargeting without separate consent, then the store avoids a purpose-limitation violation that damages trust and can breach privacy law.

signal.check: A contact detail collected for 2FA, receipts or order status shows up in a retargeting or ad audience list with no separate consent recorded.

risk.note: None; a data-use boundary check.

prerequisites: A map of where 2FA and receipt contact details flow
steps: Trace where phone numbers and emails collected for 2FA, receipts or order status are used.
Confirm none reach a retargeting or ad audience list without separate consent.
Remove any found instance and add a consent gate before this reuse happens.

test.method: Check a sample of the retargeting audience list against 2FA-only contact sources
test.measure: count of purpose-limitation violations found

title: Remove non-payment third-party tags from the checkout and payment step
hypothesis: If every third-party tag on the checkout and payment step that is not required to take payment is removed, then shopper tracking exposure and skimming surface both shrink at the highest-value, highest-risk page in the store.

signal.check: A chat widget, A/B testing tag, ad pixel or analytics tag not required for payment sits on the checkout or payment page.

risk.note: Removing a tag can affect an A/B test or attribution reading on checkout; coordinate with measurement before removing.

prerequisites: The checkout script inventory
steps: List every third-party tag on the checkout and payment step.
Flag any not required to take payment.
Remove flagged tags and confirm checkout still functions.

test.method: Recrawl the checkout page after removal and confirm only payment-required tags remain
test.measure: count of non-payment tags remaining on checkout

title: Build a quarterly security review calendar covering every checklist and its owner
hypothesis: If access audits, app audits, fraud settings review, bot defence review, privacy checks, backup restore tests, staff training and CT log review are all placed on a standing quarterly calendar with an owner and due date, then security stops being a one-time setup and becomes a maintained practice.

signal.check: Security reviews happen only when something goes wrong, with no standing quarterly calendar of checklists, owners and due dates.

risk.note: None; a calendar and ownership document.

prerequisites: The individual checklists and procedures already defined
steps: List standing entries: access audit, app and dependency audit, fraud settings review, bot defence review, privacy check, CT log review, backup restore test, staff training, disclosed-vulnerability read, threat model refresh.
Add a twice-yearly incident drill and a pre-peak-season Flow rule review.
Assign an owner and a due date to each entry.
Put the calendar somewhere the whole team can see it.

test.method: Check completion rate of calendar entries after one full quarter
test.measure: share of scheduled entries completed on time

title: Build a full store threat model weighted by peak calendar, region and past incidents
hypothesis: If the store runs a full threat model covering all threat classes, weighted by the brand's own peak calendar, EU/UK exposure and past incidents, then security spend targets the store's real risk profile instead of a generic checklist applied evenly.

signal.check: No threat model exists for the store, or the last one predates a major change (new payment method, new region, new app).

risk.note: Documentation only; no live change.

prerequisites: Platform, gateway, regions, staff, apps, scripts, order and login data, and past incidents
steps: List the 4 targets (browser, server, client app, user) and the store's threat classes.
For each, record whether it applies, the current control, the evidence it works, and the gap.
Weight by the brand's own data: past chargebacks, login failures, drop calendar, EU/UK exposure, custom code footprint, app count with customer-data access.
Add the 4-pillars column with an owner per pillar and a hosting-model row.
Mark every vendor statistic as unverified and every brand number still needed.

test.method: Check that every threat row has a control or an explicit none
test.measure: share of threat rows with a documented control or gap
test.read_point: right after the model is built, then refreshed yearly

title: Run a full Shopify security baseline review across all 12 areas in one sitting
hypothesis: If the store runs one full Shopify security baseline review (2FA, staff permissions, fraud settings, Flow, apps, checkout scripts, HTTPS, headers, DNS, card data, PCI scope, backups, privacy) in one pass, then gaps that individually seem small get caught together and prioritized instead of being addressed piecemeal over months.

signal.check: No single, dated Shopify security baseline review has ever been completed covering all 12 areas together.

risk.note: Review only; any live change found necessary goes through its own sign-off.

prerequisites: Owner or full-access staff login for the human operator running the review
steps: Confirm 2FA on every staff account and export staff permissions.
Record fraud settings, Flow workflows, and the installed app list with permissions.
Crawl checkout, cart and account pages for scripts; confirm HTTPS and check response headers.
Check registrar MFA, CAA and dangling CNAMEs; sample for card data outside checkout.
Confirm PCI scope in writing, check backups, and confirm the privacy policy and consent banner.
Fill the baseline checklist with a bad-row owner and date for every gap found.

test.method: Complete the full checklist and count bad rows with an assigned owner and date
test.measure: share of checklist rows completed with an owner
test.read_point: right after the review, then each quarter

title: Roll out the self-hosted HTTPS, HSTS, CAA and CT transport baseline in graduated steps
hypothesis: If a self-hosted store rolls out full-site HTTPS, then HSTS at a low max-age raised gradually, then CAA and Certificate Transparency monitoring, in that graduated order, then transport security reaches a mature state without the lockout risk of jumping straight to a long HSTS max-age with includeSubDomains.

signal.check: Self-hosted transport security is partial (HTTPS without HSTS, or HSTS set at a long max-age with no gradual rollout) and CAA or CT monitoring is missing.

risk.note: A long HSTS max-age cannot be undone for users who already cached it; raise gradually.

prerequisites: Control of DNS and web server headers; a list of every subdomain including vendor-run ones
steps: Confirm every hostname serves valid TLS and redirects HTTP to HTTPS; fix mixed content.
Add the HSTS header at a low max-age and watch for a full error-reporting cycle.
Raise max-age in steps toward the mature value; add includeSubDomains only once every subdomain passes.
Publish a CAA record naming only the CAs in use.
Set up Certificate Transparency log monitoring for the domain and review quarterly.

test.method: Load the site in a fresh browser profile with no history and confirm HTTPS-only with no certificate warnings
test.measure: share of hostnames passing the HTTPS-only check

title: Run the bot and agent policy rollout in 4 phases over about 3 months
hypothesis: If the store runs the bot and agent policy as a 4-phase program (assess, define policy, implement, monitor continuously) instead of flipping a block switch on day one, then enforcement matches the real traffic baseline and ships with a false-decline check built in.

signal.check: A bot policy went live with no assessment phase, no defined per-endpoint policy, and no continuous monitoring after launch.

risk.note: Ship any new block rule as monitor-only first, then challenge, then block, each with sign-off.

prerequisites: Ability to inventory current bot/WAF rules, APIs and traffic
steps: Phase 1 (weeks 1-4): document current bot and WAF rules; inventory APIs including undocumented ones; baseline agent activity.
Phase 2 (weeks 3-6): define allow/monitor/rate-limit/authenticate/block per category and endpoint; set trust tiers; define escalation thresholds.
Phase 3 (weeks 5-12): deploy behavior telemetry; integrate an agent identity protocol if accepting verified agents; build per-action authorization.
Phase 4 (ongoing): run dashboards on verification pass/fail rates; tune; red-team owned systems only.
Run a readiness self-check before and after: visibility, policy, privacy, security, with an owner per unchecked box.

test.method: Audit false declines on headless traffic after phase 3 ships
test.measure: false-decline rate on headless/API traffic with no other risk signal
test.read_point: at the end of phase 3, then ongoing

title: Run a full staff access audit and same-day offboarding process
hypothesis: If the store runs a full staff access audit producing an access matrix and a same-day offboarding rule, then stale access from agency turnover and role changes stops compounding every other security gap.

signal.check: No current access matrix exists mapping every account to a role, permissions, 2FA status and last login.

risk.note: None; a review and revocation process, with human sign-off before revoking.

prerequisites: Export capability for staff, collaborator, agency and API accounts
steps: Export every staff, collaborator, agency and API account with permissions, 2FA status and last login.
Map each to a documented role; flag full-access grants and accounts of people who left.
Time-box contractor and agency access with an end date.
Review admin login locations and alerts.
Write the access matrix and revocation list; revoke same day for anyone who leaves.

test.method: Confirm no departed person retains access after the audit
test.measure: count of departed-person accounts still active
test.read_point: right after the audit, then quarterly

title: Run a full app and dependency audit with an inventory and a clean dependency tree
hypothesis: If the store runs a full app and dependency audit (permissions, last use, lockfile diff, typosquat check, install sandbox) in one pass, then the largest attack surface specific to a hosted-platform store gets addressed together instead of app by app as problems surface.

signal.check: No dated, complete app and dependency audit exists covering permissions, unused apps and dependency hygiene together.

risk.note: Removing an app can break a workflow; confirm with the app's users before removing.

prerequisites: Access to export the installed app list and, for custom code, the dependency lockfile
steps: Export installed apps: permissions, install date, last use, developer, Built for Shopify status, review score.
Remove unused apps; confirm permissions match function for kept apps.
For custom code: diff the lockfile, review new direct dependencies, check for typosquats and maintainer changes.
Confirm installs run in a disposable, network-restricted build step.
List browser extensions on admin machines and subscribe to security bulletins.

test.method: Confirm every app has an owner and a reason, and no dependency lacks a maintainer
test.measure: share of apps and dependencies with a documented owner
test.read_point: right after the audit, then quarterly and after any checkout/payment app install

title: Run a backup and restore test end to end, not just confirm backups exist
hypothesis: If the store runs an actual restore of critical data (products, orders, customers, theme code, Flow rules) to a test environment and times it, then backup coverage is proven instead of assumed, closing the gap where 'we have backups' turns out to mean 'we have never restored one'.

signal.check: Backups run automatically but have never been restored to confirm they work.

risk.note: Restore to a test store or staging, never overwrite production during the test.

prerequisites: A test store or staging environment to restore into
steps: Define critical data: products, orders, customers, content, theme code, configuration, Flow rules.
Run a restore to a test store or staging and time it.
Record what did not restore correctly.
Set and stick to a restore-test cadence, since no source specifies one (quarterly is a reasonable placeholder).

test.method: Check restored data against a checksum or record count
test.measure: restore completeness and time to complete

title: Write and drill the incident response runbook covering breach, skimming, ATO and ransomware
hypothesis: If a single written runbook covers detect, contain, investigate, eradicate, notify and review for a breach, skimming event, ATO wave or ransomware, with named owners and contacts, then the on-call person has a plan to follow instead of improvising during the worst moment to have to improvise.

signal.check: No single written incident runbook exists naming a person per step and a contact for the processor, insurer and counsel.

risk.note: Get qualified security and legal help for a real incident; this runbook is an outline, not a substitute.

prerequisites: Contacts for the processor, acquirer, cyber insurer and counsel
steps: Detect and classify: skimming signal, credential dump, ATO wave, data exposure, ransomware.
Contain: take the affected page offline, rotate credentials (a human does it, never in chat), lock affected accounts, block the source.
Investigate: file-change logs, admin user list, payment routes, app installs, DNS records.
Eradicate and restore from a clean backup if needed.
Notify the processor, supervisory authority, customers and insurer within the legal window.
Review root cause and update the runbook.

test.method: Run a tabletop drill twice a year and time each step
test.measure: time from detection to containment in the drill

title: Set up a vulnerability disclosure intake process with a stated response and fix SLA
hypothesis: If the store sets up the full disclosure process end to end (intake channel, response SLA, embargo, classification, publication), then a security researcher reports responsibly instead of going public, and a fix ships without leaking details early.

signal.check: No documented process exists for how a reported vulnerability moves from intake to fix to public disclosure.

risk.note: None; a process to publish and follow.

prerequisites: A monitored intake channel
steps: Publish an intake channel (a security email or a platform).
Commit to a response time (about 24 hours) and update cadence (about 48 hours).
Classify with CWE, score with CVSS, then rescore for the brand's own context.
Embargo until the fix ships, binding the whole team and any contractor.
Ship the fix and publish a note, even if it breaks compatibility.

test.method: Send a test report through the process end to end and time each step
test.measure: time from report to acknowledged fix
test.read_point: on the first real report received

does_not_apply_when: A store with no custom code or public-facing app to report against

title: Run a full privacy and consent check across storefront, account and checkout pages
hypothesis: If the store runs a complete privacy and consent check (crawl every page, name every vendor and purpose, confirm the consent banner and policy) in one pass, then tracking matches disclosure across the whole site instead of only where someone happened to look.

signal.check: No single, dated privacy and consent audit exists covering storefront, account and checkout pages together.

risk.note: Removing a tag with no documented purpose can affect a feature; confirm before removing.

prerequisites: Ability to crawl storefront, account and checkout pages
steps: Crawl storefront, account and checkout pages and list every third-party request.
For each, record vendor, purpose, cookies, data observed and consent category.
Remove any tag with no owner or purpose, and any non-payment tag on the payment step.
Confirm the consent banner blocks non-essential tags before consent in the EU and UK.
Confirm purpose limitation: 2FA and order-contact details are not reused for retargeting without separate consent.

test.method: Test the consent banner from a fresh EU-located profile and recrawl for unowned tags
test.measure: count of unowned tags and banner pass/fail
test.read_point: right after the audit, then quarterly

title: Check both sides of any postMessage call before trusting the data
hypothesis: If every postMessage sender names the exact target origin and every receiver checks event.origin before using event.data, then a widget or iframe cannot leak account details to any embedding site or accept a forged message from an attacker.
does_not_apply_when: No cross-origin postMessage calls exist in the storefront code

signal.check: A postMessage call uses a wildcard target origin, or a message listener reads event.data before checking event.origin.

risk.note: None; this only adds a check.

prerequisites: A list of every postMessage sender and listener in the storefront and any embedded widgets
steps: List every place the storefront sends or listens for postMessage.
For each sender, pass the exact destination origin, never a wildcard.
For each listener, check event.origin against the expected value before using event.data.
Test with a page from a different origin to confirm a forged message is rejected.

test.method: Send a test message from an unrelated origin to each listener
test.measure: whether the forged message is rejected

title: Replace JSONP with a CORS endpoint or server-side proxy for partner data
hypothesis: If a JSONP call to a partner or marketplace API is replaced with a CORS-enabled endpoint or a server-side proxy, then a compromised partner API can no longer run arbitrary script on the storefront page.
does_not_apply_when: No JSONP calls exist anywhere in the storefront or theme code

signal.check: A storefront page loads a script tag with a callback query parameter to read data from a partner or affiliate API.

risk.note: Removing JSONP does not change the data shown once the replacement call works.

prerequisites: A list of every JSONP call in theme, app or custom code
steps: Grep theme and app code for callback query parameters and script tags built from a partner URL.
Ask the partner for a CORS-enabled JSON endpoint or existing API key access.
If no CORS endpoint exists, fetch the data server-side and re-serve it from the store's own origin.
Remove the JSONP script tag once the replacement call is confirmed working.

test.method: Compare the data shown before and after the switch on a staging page
test.measure: page renders the same data with no JSONP script tag present

title: Add rel=noopener to every outbound target=_blank link
hypothesis: If every outbound link that opens a new tab carries rel=noopener, then the new tab cannot silently redirect the original storefront or blog tab to a fake login page.

signal.check: An outbound link to an external site uses target=_blank with no rel=noopener or rel=noreferrer attribute.

risk.note: None; this only removes a back-reference the new tab does not need.

prerequisites: Access to the theme, blog and email templates that render outbound links
steps: Grep templates and content for target=_blank links to external domains.
Add rel=noopener and rel=noreferrer to each one, or set it in the shared link-rendering component.
Cover blog posts, reviews, help articles and any user-generated content with outbound links.
Recheck after any theme or CMS update, since a new template can reintroduce the gap.

test.method: Open an outbound link and confirm the new tab has no window.opener reference back
test.measure: share of outbound target=_blank links carrying rel=noopener
test.read_point: right after the fix ships, then after each theme update

title: Hex-encode or use a template tag for data inside inline script blocks
hypothesis: If untrusted data placed inside an inline script block is hex-encoded and decoded at runtime, or moved into an inert template tag instead, then a literal closing script tag in the data cannot break out and inject a new script block.
does_not_apply_when: No untrusted data is ever written directly into an inline script block

signal.check: Server-rendered code writes a user-controlled value directly into an inline script block using only quote or backslash escaping.

risk.note: None; this changes how a value is encoded, not what it displays.

prerequisites: A list of every place untrusted data is written into an inline script block
steps: Find every inline script block that includes a user-controlled or request-derived value.
Hex-encode the value before embedding it, and decode it back to the real value at runtime in JS.
Where practical, move the value into an inert template tag instead and read it via the DOM at runtime.
Test with a payload containing a literal closing script tag and confirm it cannot start a new script block.

test.method: Submit a value containing a closing script tag to each affected field and inspect the rendered page source
test.measure: whether the literal closing tag breaks out of the script block

title: Monitor Safe Browsing status for the storefront domain
hypothesis: If the store registers for Safe Browsing or search-console alerts on its own domain, then a malware or phishing flag on the storefront is caught and fixed within hours instead of being found later through lost traffic and a support backlog.

signal.check: No one has registered the storefront domain for Safe Browsing or search-console security alerts, so a flag would only be found when a customer or browser warning is reported.

risk.note: None; this is monitoring, not a live change.

prerequisites: Ownership verification of the storefront domain with the search console or webmaster tool used
steps: Verify domain ownership in a search console or webmaster tool that reports Safe Browsing status.
Turn on security-issue email alerts for the domain.
Assign a named person to act on any alert the same day it arrives.
Test the alert path once, then review quarterly that alerts are still delivered.

test.method: Confirm the alert email address is current and receives a test notification
test.measure: time from a flag being raised to a person acting on it

title: Allow password paste and recommend a password manager to customers
hypothesis: If login and password fields allow paste and autofill, and the store points customers to a password manager, then customers can use long unique passwords instead of weak reused ones, and phishing succeeds less often because a password manager only fills on the real origin.

signal.check: The password or confirm-password field blocks paste, or autofill does not work, on the login, registration or checkout account fields.

risk.note: None; removing a paste block does not weaken any other control.

prerequisites: Access to the login, registration and checkout account form code
steps: Test whether paste and autofill work on every password field: login, registration, checkout, password reset.
Remove any JavaScript that blocks paste into a password field.
Add a short help-center note recommending a password manager for the store account.
Confirm autofill still works after any theme or checkout update.

test.method: Copy a generated password and paste it into each password field on staging
test.measure: share of password fields that accept paste and autofill

title: Offer passwordless passkey login as an option for customer accounts
hypothesis: If customer accounts can sign in with a WebAuthn passkey instead of a password, then account takeover from phishing and credential stuffing drops for customers who enroll, because a passkey only works on the real origin and never leaves the device.
does_not_apply_when: The platform gives no way to add passkey or WebAuthn login to customer accounts

signal.check: Customer accounts can only sign in with a password, and the platform or a plugin supports passkey login that is not turned on.

risk.note: Decide the account recovery path before rollout, since a lost device with no fallback locks the customer out.

prerequisites: Platform or plugin support for WebAuthn or passkey customer login
A decided account recovery path
steps: Confirm whether the platform or an app supports passkey login for customer accounts.
Decide the recovery path for a customer who loses their passkey device before turning it on.
Offer the passkey as an option alongside the password, not a forced replacement, at first.
Track enrollment and login success rate for passkey versus password customers.
Promote the option on the account page once it is confirmed working end to end.

test.method: Enroll a test account with a passkey and complete a full login and checkout
test.measure: passkey enrollment rate and login success rate versus password login

title: Run automated dependency vulnerability scanning on every build
hypothesis: If every build runs an automated dependency vulnerability scan, then a package with a known security flaw is caught before release instead of relying only on someone reading changelogs or security bulletins.
does_not_apply_when: The store has no custom codebase or build pipeline to scan

signal.check: No automated tool checks installed dependencies against known-vulnerability data; the only check is manual changelog reading.

risk.note: None; scanning does not change running code by itself.

prerequisites: A build or CI pipeline the scanning tool can run in
steps: Add an automated dependency vulnerability scan, for example npm audit or a Dependabot-style tool, to the build pipeline.
Set the pipeline to fail or flag the build on a high-severity known vulnerability.
Assign a named person to triage and fix or accept each flagged finding.
Review the scan's findings history monthly to confirm alerts are being acted on.

test.method: Introduce a dependency with a known flaw on a test branch and confirm the scan flags it
test.measure: whether the scan catches the planted vulnerability
test.read_point: right after the scan is added

title: Change default credentials and update firmware on store network devices
hypothesis: If routers, POS terminals, cameras and printers on the store network get their default admin credentials changed, are kept off the open internet, and run current firmware, then they stop being an easy target for botnets and local network attackers.

signal.check: A router, POS terminal, camera or printer on the store network still uses its default admin password, is reachable directly from the internet, or has not been updated in over a year.

risk.note: None; this only removes default access and closes exposure.

prerequisites: A list of every network device at the store or warehouse
steps: List every router, POS terminal, camera, printer and other networked device the store operates.
Change every device's admin password from its factory default.
Confirm none of these devices is reachable directly from the open internet.
Check each device's firmware version and update it, or replace devices no longer supported.
Repeat the check yearly or after adding any new device.

test.method: Scan the store network for default-credential logins and any device reachable from outside
test.measure: count of devices still on default credentials or open to the internet
test.read_point: right after the fix, then yearly

title: Remove document.domain relaxation and use postMessage instead
hypothesis: If any use of document.domain to relax the Same-Origin Policy is removed and replaced with explicit postMessage communication, then a compromise of one subdomain can no longer silently reach into every other subdomain that opted into the same relaxed domain.
does_not_apply_when: No code sets document.domain anywhere in the storefront or its subdomains

signal.check: Any page under the store's domain sets document.domain to relax the Same-Origin Policy for cross-subdomain access.

risk.note: None; this removes a legacy pattern and replaces it with an equivalent one.

prerequisites: Access to the source of every subdomain under the store's main domain
steps: Grep every subdomain's codebase for document.domain.
Treat any match as a finding to fix, not a pattern to keep.
Replace the cross-subdomain communication it enabled with postMessage, checking origin on both sides.
Confirm the replaced flow still works end to end after the change.

test.method: Grep production code for document.domain after the change
test.measure: count of remaining document.domain occurrences

title: Strip CORS access-control headers from endpoints that should not share data
hypothesis: If a broad cross-origin sharing header is removed from any API endpoint that was never meant to share its response with another site's script, then a different origin can no longer read customer or order data through a permissive CORS header.
does_not_apply_when: No custom API endpoints set CORS headers

signal.check: An endpoint returning customer, order or account data sets a wildcard or broad cross-origin sharing header with no real cross-origin need.

risk.note: Removing a CORS header can break a legitimate integration that relies on it; confirm nothing needs it first.

prerequisites: A list of every API endpoint and its current CORS response headers
steps: List every endpoint and check its cross-origin sharing response header, if any.
For each one, confirm whether a real, named cross-origin caller needs it.
Remove the header from any endpoint with no confirmed cross-origin need, especially ones returning customer or order data.
Narrow any remaining header from a wildcard to the exact origin that needs it.

test.method: Fetch each sensitive endpoint from a test page on a different origin before and after the change
test.measure: whether the cross-origin fetch can read the response

title: Stream large file downloads instead of buffering them in memory
hypothesis: If large downloads such as order exports, invoices and media files are streamed to the client instead of loaded fully into server memory first, then a burst of large-file requests cannot exhaust server memory and take down the store.
does_not_apply_when: The store serves no large files itself; all media and exports are served from a CDN or third-party storage

signal.check: A download or export endpoint reads the whole file into memory before sending it, instead of streaming it to the response.

risk.note: None; streaming produces the same file to the client.

prerequisites: A list of every endpoint that serves a large file: exports, invoices, media, backups
steps: List every endpoint that serves a large file: exports, invoices, media, backups.
For each one, confirm whether the code buffers the whole file before sending it.
Switch any buffering endpoint to a streaming response.
Load-test the endpoint with concurrent large-file requests and watch server memory.

test.method: Request several large files concurrently on staging and watch server memory usage
test.measure: peak server memory during concurrent large-file requests, before and after the change
